groups.title: Time gap / headway and standstill gap

claims.quantity: Net time gap ('gap headway') in close car-following on UK motorways, all lanes, all vehicle types
claims.value: mean about 1.1 s, SD 0.42 s. The sample keeps only pairs with gap headway <= 2 s and a speed difference < 1.5 m/s, so the distribution is truncated at 2 s
claims.region: UK (M25 J15-16, M42 J5-6, loop detectors, Managed Motorways)
claims.source: Al-Obaedi, J.T.S. (2019). Close Following Behavior: Estimation of Desired Gap Headway Using Loop Detector Data. International Journal of Engineering (IJE), Transactions B: Applications, 32(5), 661-666
claims.quote: suggested that the mean gap headway of drivers is about 1.1 s with standard deviation of 0.42 s

check.corrected_value: Mean about 1.1 s, SD 0.42 s. The paper's Summary and Section 3.1 tie this to speeds of about 70 km/h and above (Eq. 2 uses 1.1 s for speed > 70 km/h). Vehicles above 100 km/h were also excluded. The paper never says this is an all-lanes, all-vehicle-types figure.
check.note: The abstract quote is verbatim. The filters (gap headway <= 2 s, speed difference <= 1.5 m/s, M25 J15-16 and M42 J5-6 Managed Motorways, 14 days, more than 250k pairs) are confirmed in Section 2. The Summary says 'about 1.1 s with standard deviation of 0.42 s at that speed', meaning up to/at 70 km/h, so the value depends on speed and is not an overall pooled mean.

claims.quantity: Net time gap in close following, M25 middle lane, speeds 60-100 km/h
claims.value: mean about 1.15 s, SD 0.43 s; min 0.2 s, max 2.0 s (the maximum is the filter cap)
claims.source: Al-Obaedi, J.T.S. (2019). Close Following Behavior: Estimation of Desired Gap Headway Using Loop Detector Data. IJE Trans. B 32(5), 661-666
claims.quote: from 60 to 100km/h were about 1.15s with standard deviation of 0.43 s

check.note: Section 3.1, p. 663, M25 middle lane (Lane 2), Fig. 2: 'about 1.15s with standard deviation of 0.43 s. The maximum and minimum values were 0.2 and 2.0 s'. The 2.0 s maximum matches the 2 s filter cap.

claims.quantity: Speed dependence of the close-following net time gap (congested to near-capacity speeds)
claims.value: about 1.5 s at an average speed of 15 km/h; about 1.1 s at 75 km/h. Offside lanes are lower than inside lanes above 70 km/h
claims.source: Al-Obaedi, J.T.S. (2019). Close Following Behavior: Estimation of Desired Gap Headway Using Loop Detector Data. IJE Trans. B 32(5), 661-666
claims.quote: the average desired gap headway for average speed of 15km/h is about 1.5 s, while the average gap headway is 1.1 s for the speed of 75km/h

check.note: The quote is verbatim in Section 3.1 (M25, Fig. 2). Section 3.2 (M42, Fig. 4) says offside lanes choose lower gap headways than inside lanes above 70 km/h and similar values below 70 km/h. Eq. 2 gives GH = 1.5 - 0.006·speed below 70 km/h.

claims.quantity: Lower tail of the close-following net time gap distribution (M42, 60-80 km/h)
claims.value: about 15 % of drivers at <= 0.5 s. The author fits a Normal distribution (Fig. 5) and recommends sampling from the empirical CDF
claims.source: Al-Obaedi, J.T.S. (2019). Close Following Behavior: Estimation of Desired Gap Headway Using Loop Detector Data. IJE Trans. B 32(5), 661-666
claims.quote: about 15 percent of drivers maintain gap headway of 0.5 s or less

check.corrected_value: About 15 % at <= 0.5 s (M42, 60-70 and 70-80 km/h, Fig. 5 empirical CDF; same on M25). The author does NOT fit a Normal in Fig. 5. Fig. 6 compares the histogram with a Normal, finds it left-skewed, and rejects normality at 95 %. He then recommends sampling Fig. 5 with uniform random numbers.
check.note: The 15 % figure and the empirical-CDF recommendation are correct. Saying a Normal was fitted in Fig. 5 is wrong: normality was tested and rejected (Section 3.3).

claims.quantity: Difference in close-following net time gap between HGV followers and small-car followers (60-70 km/h)
claims.value: 70th percentile for HGVs is < 0.1 s higher than for small cars; K-S test not significant at 95 %. This holds within the <= 2 s close-following filter only
claims.region: UK (M42/M25; HGVs banned from the offside lanes)
claims.source: Al-Obaedi, J.T.S. (2019). Close Following Behavior: Estimation of Desired Gap Headway Using Loop Detector Data. IJE Trans. B 32(5), 661-666
claims.quote: the 70th percentile of gap headway for HGVs drivers is only higher than that for “small cars” drivers by less than 0.1 s

check.note: The quote is verbatim in Section 3.4, Fig. 7 (60-70 km/h). The K-S test at 95 % confidence found the difference insignificant. Section 2 confirms HGVs are banned from the offside lanes. The result is within the <= 2 s close-following filter.

claims.quantity: Most probable net ('netto') time gap by density regime, with car/truck pairs separated
claims.value: mode 0.75 s in free traffic (fast lane). Upstream of a bottleneck (Loop 4): 1.2 s at medium density (25-50 veh/km/lane) and 1.9 s at high density (>50). Slow-lane values somewhat higher. Truck-follower gaps behind cars are considerably higher on average (truck = length >= 6 m)
claims.source: Nishinari, K., Treiber, M., Helbing, D. Interpreting the Wide Scattering of Synchronized Traffic Data by Time Gap Statistics. arXiv:cond-mat/0212295v2 (2004)
claims.quote: from 0.75 s in free traffic (on the fast lane) to considerably higher values in congested traffic upstream of a bottleneck (1.2 s at medium densitities and 1.9 s at high densities at Loop 4

check.note: The Fig. 2 caption (A9, double-loop single-vehicle data) gives the most probable netto gap: 0.75 s in free traffic on the fast lane, 1.2 s at medium (25-50 veh/km/lane) and 1.9 s at high (>50) density at Loop 4, and slow lane somewhat higher. Trucks are defined as length >= 6 m, and truck gaps behind cars are 'considerably higher' on average. Also: Loop 12 stays at 0.75 s in all regimes, and Loop 7 is 1 s at medium density.

claims.quantity: Average net time gap in dense synchronized flow (density >= 45 veh/km/lane)
claims.value: T = 2.25 s; SD of the 50-vehicle-averaged T = 0.29 s. This is not the SD between individuals
claims.source: Nishinari, K., Treiber, M., Helbing, D. Interpreting the Wide Scattering of Synchronized Traffic Data by Time Gap Statistics. arXiv:cond-mat/0212295v2 (2004)
claims.quote: T = 2.25 s the average time gap, and ∆T = 0.29 s the standard deviation of T

check.note: Fig. 1 caption: 'T = 2.25 s the average time gap, and ∆T = 0.29 s the standard deviation of T', for density >= 45 veh/km/lane. T is the average over N = 50 successive vehicles (Eq. 3), so ∆T is the spread of 50-vehicle means, not between individuals.

claims.quantity: Gross time headway distribution in free flow, left lane, motorway without a speed limit
claims.value: mode about 0.68 s, nearly independent of density; a non-negligible share around 0.2 s. With a speed limit the mode shifts to larger values. The paper warns that older single-vehicle data had 0.9 s buffer artefacts
claims.region: Germany (A3 near Duisburg, no speed limit; A1 near Köln)
claims.source: Knospe, W., Santen, L., Schadschneider, A., Schreckenberg, M. Single-vehicle data of highway traffic: microscopic description of traffic phases. arXiv:cond-mat/0203347v1 (2002)
claims.quote: Not only the maximum of the distribution is at about 0.68 s, but also the values of the shortest time-headways do not change significantly.

check.note: Fig. 10: left lane, detector D1 on the A3 (no speed limit), free flow. The text says the distribution narrows with density but the maximum stays at about 0.68 s. The paper also says 'a non-negligible portion of vehicles drives with a temporal distance of the order ~0.2 s', that a speed limit shifts the maximum to larger headways, and that the earlier 1.8 s peak came from a 0.9 s detector buffer artefact. The inset is from the A1 near Köln-Lövenich.

claims.quantity: Per-driver mean steady-state time gap (rear of leader to front of follower) by speed, naturalistic
claims.value: 7 drivers. At 90-108 km/h the driver means are 0.98-1.68 s (COV 23.9-50.4 %); at >= 108 km/h 0.97-1.86 s (COV up to 63.8 %); at 18-36 km/h 1.53-2.67 s. Pooled median about 2.5 s at 18-36 km/h and 1.2 s at 90-108 km/h
claims.region: US (Dulles Airport access road, Washington DC; 168,053 samples)
claims.source: Loulizi, A., Bichiou, Y., Rakha, H. (2019). Steady-State Car-Following Time Gaps: An Empirical Study Using Naturalistic Driving Data. Journal of Advanced Transportation, 2019, 7659496
claims.quote: at a speed interval of [18, 36[, the median is about 2.5 s but drops to 1.2 s at a speed interval of [90, 108[

check.note: Table 2 (p. 5) matches: [90,108[ means 0.98-1.68 s with COV 23.9-50.4 %; >=108 means 0.97-1.86 s with COV up to 63.8 % (Driver 462); [18,36[ means 1.53-2.67 s. The pooled medians of about 2.5 s and 1.2 s are verbatim in Section 4.2. The gap is measured rear of leader to front of follower. Seven drivers, Dulles access road, 168,053 samples.

claims.quantity: Best-fit distribution of the pooled steady-state time gap at 90-108 km/h
claims.value: Pearson 5 with shape α = 7.75, scale β = 8.78 s, location γ = 0 (K-S best fit). I computed the implied mean as β/(α−1) ≈ 1.30 s. Other speed bins use other families (Johnson SB, Pert, Kumaraswamy). The authors recommend empirical distributions over fitted ones
claims.source: Loulizi, A., Bichiou, Y., Rakha, H. (2019). Steady-State Car-Following Time Gaps: An Empirical Study Using Naturalistic Driving Data. Journal of Advanced Transportation, 2019, 7659496
claims.quote: [90–108[ Pearson 5 Scale parameter: 𝛽 = 8.78 ... Location parameter: 𝛾 = 0

check.corrected_value: Pearson 5 with α = 7.75, β = 8.78, γ = 0 (top K-S rank for [90,108[). The implied mean β/(α−1) ≈ 1.30 s is arithmetically right. However, with all 88,692 samples the fit is rejected by K-S, χ² and A-D at 0.01. It passes K-S only after down-sampling to <= 10 % (8,861 points; Table 5). The authors say empirical distributions 'could be used' in microsimulation; they do not recommend them over fitted ones.
check.note: The parameters and the other families (Johnson SB, Pearson 6, Pert, Kumaraswamy) are confirmed in Table 4. The 'best fit' label hides that the fit is statistically rejected at the full sample size. The 'recommend' wording overstates conclusion (6).

claims.quantity: Share of 10-s motorway intervals with a mean time gap < 1 s (Dutch naturalistic study; manual baseline and ACC+LKS pooled)
claims.value: 33.6 % of the intervals with a lead vehicle (1,887 of 5,622). Pooled across manual and ACC conditions. Drivers were less likely to have a gap < 1 s with ACC+LKS active
claims.region: Netherlands (motorways; BMW 5 series and Tesla Model S)
claims.source: Varotto, S.F., Mons, C., Hogema, J.H., Christoph, M., van Nes, N., Martens, M.H. (2022). Do adaptive cruise control and lane keeping systems make the longitudinal vehicle control safer? ... Transportation Research Part C 141, 103756
claims.quote: had a time gap shorter than one second in 33.6% of the intervals (1,887 10-s intervals)

check.note: Section 3.1: 7,175 valid 10-s intervals; a lead vehicle was present in 5,622 of them; the time gap was < 1 s in 33.6 % (1,887). Six system states (manual, ACC and/or LKS) are pooled. 10 drivers, motorways with a limit >= 100 km/h. The abstract says drivers were less likely to have a < 1 s gap with ACC+LKS. This is not a pure HDV sample.

claims.quantity: Time headway to the preceding vehicle at lane-change events, cars vs heavy vehicles (not steady car-following)
claims.value: Cars: mean 1.53 s, SD 1.05, min 0.21, P25 0.80, median 1.20, P75 1.93, max 8.14. Heavy vehicles: mean 2.76 s, SD 2.36, min 0.27, P25 0.99, median 1.92, P75 3.90, max 13.08. Samples: 7,674 cars and 746 heavy vehicles
claims.source: Li, Y., Li, L., Ni, D. Exploration of lane-changing duration for heavy vehicles and passenger cars: a survival analysis approach. arXiv:2108.05710
claims.locator: Table 1 and the text under Fig. 4
claims.quote: The mean time-headway of heavy vehicles and passenger cars is about 2.76s and 1.53s.

check.note: All values match Table 1 (cars 1.53/1.05/0.21/0.80/1.20/1.93/8.14; heavy vehicles 2.76/2.36/0.27/0.99/1.92/3.90/13.08), with 746 heavy-vehicle and 7,674 car trajectories. These are headways during lane-change events in highD, not steady car-following.

claims.quantity: Average minimum time headway kept on instruction ('minimum safe distance'), 50-100 km/h (as cited)
claims.value: 0.64-0.69 s, nearly constant with speed (distance 9.5 m at 50 km/h to 19 m at 100 km/h)
claims.source: Loulizi, Bichiou, Rakha (2019), J. Adv. Transp. 2019:7659496, citing Taieb-Maimon & Shinar (2001), Human Factors 43(1) [original not read: VERIFY]
claims.locator: Loulizi et al., Section 1 literature review (p. 3)
claims.quote: resulted in an average minimum time headway nearly constant with speed and ranging from 0.64 s to 0.69 s

check.note: The quote is verbatim in Loulizi et al. p. 3 (9.5 m at 50 km/h to 19 m at 100 km/h; 0.64-0.69 s), citing ref [39] Taieb-Maimon & Shinar, Human Factors 43(1):159-172, 2001. This is a secondary citation only. Loulizi does not state the country; the original was not read.

claims.quantity: Mean net time gap in following above 55 km/h, instrumented vehicle (as cited); effect of leader type
claims.value: about 1.25 s (cited by Al-Obaedi). The abstract snippet says subjects followed trucks more closely than cars and that flow had little effect
claims.source: Al-Obaedi (2019), IJE 32(5), citing Brackstone, M., Waterson, B., McDonald, M. (2009). Determinants of following headway in congested traffic. Transportation Research Part F 12(2) [original full text blocked: VERIFY]
claims.quote: reported that the mean gap headway is about 1.25 s for speeds higher than 55km/h

check.corrected_value: About 1.25 s for speeds > 55 km/h (instrumented vehicle, limited sample), as cited by Al-Obaedi ref [3]. The statement that subjects followed trucks more closely and that flow had little effect could not be checked. Al-Obaedi only says Brackstone et al. found no significant effect of 'Vans'.
check.note: The 1.25 s citation is verbatim on Al-Obaedi p. 662. Al-Obaedi lists ref [3] with the title 'Determinants of following distance in congested traffic', TRF 12(2) 131-142. I could not open the Brackstone abstract because this session's web-search budget was used up, so the truck/flow part is unverified.

claims.quantity: Recommended minimum time gap for drivers on high-speed roads (driving code advice)
claims.value: >= 2 s gap; at least doubled on wet roads
claims.source: The Highway Code, Rule 126 (GOV.UK)
claims.quote: allow at least a two-second gap between you and the vehicle in front on high-speed roads

check.note: GOV.UK Rule 126: 'at least a two-second gap ... on high-speed roads', 'at least doubled on wet roads and up to ten times greater on icy roads'. The rule also gives a four-second gap for large vehicles in tunnels.

claims.quantity: Legal minimum distance for trucks > 3.5 t and buses on Autobahnen above 50 km/h
claims.value: 50 m minimum distance (a fixed distance, not a time gap)
claims.source: Straßenverkehrs-Ordnung (StVO 2013), § 4 Abstand, Abs. 3
claims.quote: wenn die Geschwindigkeit mehr als 50 km/h beträgt, zu vorausfahrenden Fahrzeugen einen Mindestabstand von 50 m einhalten

check.note: StVO § 4 Abs. 3: drivers of a Lastkraftwagen over 3.5 t zulässige Gesamtmasse or a Kraftomnibus must keep a Mindestabstand of 50 m on Autobahnen above 50 km/h. This is a distance, not a time gap.

claims.quantity: Jam spacing (Newell parameter d*, includes vehicle length) per driver in congestion
claims.value: about 180 pairs. Most d* values are 5-9 m (mean vehicle length 4.5 m, so the standstill gap is roughly 0.5-4.5 m). 10 % have d* below their vehicle length; 5 % have d* > 10 m, all heavy vehicles. Two example pairs: d* 7.4-8.5 m with Newell τ 1.2-1.6 s
claims.source: Duret, A. Measurement of variability involved in the car-following rules. ECTRI Young Researchers Seminar paper, Session 3 Traffic (2), LICIT ENTPE/INRETS
claims.quote: most of the d * -values are comprised between 5 and 9 meters: this is consistent with the physical meaning of this parameter (mean vehicle length equal 4.5m)

check.note: Section 5 Discussion (p. 10): about 180 couples on lane 2; most d* are 5-9 m (mean vehicle length 4.5 m); 10 % have d* below their vehicle length; 5 % have d* > 10 m, all heavy vehicles. Table 1 couple values: d* 7.4/7.6 and 7.8/8.5 m, τ 1.6/1.4 and 1.2/1.2 s. NGSIM I-80. The 0.5-4.5 m standstill gap is the claimant's inference, not the paper's.

claims.quantity: Inter-vehicle spacing in stopped queues (definition not stated in the abstract; read beside CORSIM's 0.915 m between-vehicle value it is likely the bumper-to-bumper gap)
claims.value: average 3.66 m (12 ft), with no significant difference between sites. Compare the design value of 7.6 m per vehicle including length, and CORSIM's 0.915 m
claims.source: Long, G. (2002). Intervehicle Spacings and Queue Characteristics. Transportation Research Record 1796, 86-96
claims.quote: intervehicle spacings were found to average 3.66 m (12 ft)

check.note: The TRID abstract (TRR 1796, 86-96, 2002, doi 10.3141/1796-10) says intervehicle spacings 'average 3.66 m (12 ft)' and 'were not found to differ significantly at different sites'. It calls 7.6 m (25 ft) per vehicle and CORSIM's 0.915 m (3 ft) severe underestimates. The abstract does not define bumper-to-bumper explicitly.

claims.quantity: SUMO meaning and defaults of tau and minGap
claims.value: tau default 1.0 s: 'desired (minimum) time headway'; for Krauss it is based on the net space (leader back to follower front). minGap default 2.5 m for passenger, truck, trailer and bus
claims.source: SUMO documentation: Definition of Vehicles, Vehicle Types, and Routes; Vehicle Type Parameter Defaults
claims.locator: Car-following model parameters table; Vehicle_Type_Parameter_Defaults page
claims.quote: The driver's desired (minimum) time headway. Exact interpretation varies by model.

check.note: The SUMO docs give tau default 1 with this description: 'The driver's desired (minimum) time headway. Exact interpretation varies by model. For the default model Krauss this is based on the net space between leader back and follower front'. The Vehicle Type Parameter Defaults page lists minGap 2.5 m for passenger, truck, trailer and bus. These are the current online docs; the 1.27.1 docs were not checked separately.

claims.quantity: Commercial ACC time headway at the shortest setting, motorway platoons (campaign N.1)
claims.value: distribution peaks about 0.9 s (Hyundai Ioniq) and 1.3 s (Volvo XC40)
claims.source: Makridis, M., Mattas, K., Anesiadou, A., Ciuffo, B. openACC. An open database of car-following experiments to study the properties of commercial ACC systems. arXiv:2004.06342 (preprint of the Transportation Research Part C paper)
claims.quote: have peak values around 0.9s and 1.3s for the Hyundai and the Volvo respectively

check.note: Section 4.1: 'peak values around 0.9s and 1.3s for the Hyundai and the Volvo respectively' at the shortest settings, campaign N.1 Ispra-Cherasco. The distributions are in Appendix A, Fig. 14.

claims.quantity: Commercial ACC prevalent time headway at the shortest setting (campaign N.2)
claims.value: KIA Niro 1.1 s; Mitsubishi Outlander PHEV 1.5 s; Ford S-Max 1.3 s; VW Golf E 1.4 s; Peugeot 3008 1.1 s. Long upper tails come from cut-ins
claims.source: Makridis, Mattas, Anesiadou, Ciuffo. openACC ... arXiv:2004.06342
claims.quote: The prevalent value for the ACC controller of the KIA was 1.1s, for the Mitsubishi 1.5s, for the Ford 1.3s, for the Golf 1.4s and for the Peugeot 1.1s.

check.note: The quote is verbatim in Section 4.1 (Fig. 8, campaign N.2 Ispra-Vicolungo). The shortest setting was used because of cut-ins, which explains the long upper tails.

claims.quantity: Commercial ACC time headway at the minimum and maximum settings (campaign N.3, test track)
claims.value: min/max setting peaks: Tesla Model 3 1.3/2.7 s; BMW X5 1.2/2.5 s; Audi A6 1.2/3.5 s; Mercedes A 1.2/2.5 s. Overall conclusion: minimum and maximum about 1 s and 2.5 s. Human and ACC ranges are both roughly 1-4 s, but the human distributions are more uniform
claims.source: Makridis, Mattas, Anesiadou, Ciuffo. openACC ... arXiv:2004.06342
claims.quote: The peak values found for each vehicles are 1.3s and 2.7s for the Tesla, 1.2s and 2.5s for the BMW, 1.2s and 3.5s for the Audi and 1.2s and 2.5s for the Mercedes.

check.note: Section 4.4, Fig. 11 (AstaZero): the quoted peak pairs are verbatim. The human distributions are 'much more uniform', and both the human and ACC ranges are roughly 1-4 s. The conclusions say minimum and maximum headway values are around 1 s and 2.5 s.

claims.quantity: Commercial ACC time headway at the minimum and maximum settings; controller response time
claims.value: minimum setting a bit over 1 s; maximum setting up to 3.5 s; response time 1.7-2.5 s
claims.region: Europe (JRC campaign; exact site not read)
claims.source: Makridis, M., Mattas, K., Ciuffo, B., Re, F., Kriston, A., Minarini, F., Rognelund, G. (2020). Empirical study on the properties of adaptive cruise control systems and their impact on traffic flow and string stability. Transportation Research Record (DOI 10.1177/0361198120911047)
claims.quote: The time headway with the minimum setting and normal driving conditions is a bit over 1s

check.note: The JRC repository abstract (DOI 10.1177/0361198120911047) says: 'a bit over 1s for all the vehicles', 'with the maximum setting it can reach 3.5s', and a 'response time range ... between 1.7s and 2.5s'.

claims.quantity: Fitted effective time gap th of a constant-time-gap ACC model (s = η + th·v) at the min and max following settings, 7 vehicle models
claims.source: Gunter, G., Gloudemans, D., Stern, R.E., et al. Are commercially implemented adaptive cruise control systems string stable? arXiv:1905.02108v1 (2019)
claims.locator: Table II and text below it
claims.quote: The effective time gap th of the models range between 0.544 s and 2.054 s.

check.note: Table II th values: min settings 0.819, 0.725, 0.907, 0.544, 1.127, 0.696, 0.549; max settings 1.734-2.054. The text gives the 0.544-2.054 s range and a sensor lag of 0.153-0.994 s. Seven 2018 model-year vehicles from two makes.

claims.quantity: Fitted jam space gap η (standstill gap) of the ACC model
claims.value: 5.131-14.956 m across vehicles and settings. Vehicles A-D disengage below 25 mph, so for them η is a theoretical, not physically reached, gap
claims.source: Gunter, G., et al. Are commercially implemented adaptive cruise control systems string stable? arXiv:1905.02108v1 (2019)
claims.quote: the values for the jam space gap η range from 5.131 m for the maximum setting for Vehicle G to 14.956 m for the maximum setting for Vehicle D

check.note: The text below Table II gives η from 5.131 m (Vehicle G, max setting) to 14.956 m (Vehicle D, max setting). It says that because Vehicles A-D disengage below 25 mph, these spacings are not physically attainable and are theoretical.

claims.quantity: Time lag τ and safety buffer Δ (standstill-like gap) of a commercial ACC at its 4 headway settings
claims.source: Shi, X., Li, X. (2021). Empirical study on car-following characteristics of commercial automated vehicles with different headway settings. Transportation Research Part C 128, 103134
claims.quote: High Speed-Headway Setting 4               2.17             0.07          0.66

check.note: Table 3 (p. 7) values match exactly. The high-speed range is [8.94, 24.59] m/s and the low-speed range [8.94, 15.65] m/s. Eq. (1), ÿ = k[x − l − Δ − y − τẏ], gives an equilibrium spacing of l + Δ + τv. Lincoln MKZ 2016/2017, TR-C 128:103134.

claims.quantity: Available ACC and CACC time-gap settings on the PATH prototype cars
claims.value: CACC: 1.1, 0.9, 0.7, 0.6 s. ACC on the same vehicles: 2.2, 1.6, 1.1 s
claims.source: Shladover, S., Nowakowski, C., Cody, D., Bu, F., O'Connell, J., Spring, J., Dickey, S., Nelson, D. (2009). Effect of Cooperative Adaptive Cruise Control on Traffic Flow: Testing Drivers' Choices of Following Distances. Caltrans CA09-0818 / UCB-ITS-PPR-2009-23
claims.locator: Section 3, DVI description (PDF p. 39); Executive summary (PDF p. 9)
claims.quote: CACC time gap settings are 1.1, 0.9, 0.7 and 0.6 seconds (compared to 2.2, 1.6 and 1.1 seconds for the ACC on these vehicles)

check.note: The quote is verbatim on PDF p. 39 (DVI description). The executive summary gives CACC 0.6-1.1 s vs ACC 1.1-2.2 s. Report CA09-0818 / UCB-ITS-PPR-2009-23.

claims.quantity: Distribution of ACC time-gap settings chosen by general-public drivers in car-following (field test)
claims.source: Shladover, S.E., Lu, X.-Y., Nowakowski, C., Su, D. (2011). Development and Evaluation of Selected Mobility Applications for VII. Caltrans CA11-2138 / UCB-ITS-PRR-2011-08
claims.quote: ACC: 31.1% at 2.2 s time gap, 18.5% at 1.6 s time gap, 50.4% at 1.1 s time gap

check.note: The quote is verbatim in Section 13 before Figure 13.1 (report p. 60). Drivers were naive members of the general public, in car-following.

claims.quantity: Distribution of CACC time-gap settings chosen by general-public drivers (field test)
claims.value: 0.6 s: 57 %; 0.7 s: 24 %; 0.9 s: 7 %; 1.1 s: 12 %. Mean CACC gap = 45 % of the mean ACC gap
claims.source: Shladover, S.E., Lu, X.-Y., Nowakowski, C., Su, D. (2011). Development and Evaluation of Selected Mobility Applications for VII. Caltrans CA11-2138
claims.quote: CACC: 12% at 1.1 s time gap, 7% at 0.9 s time gap, 24% at 0.7 s time gap, 57% at 0.6 s time gap.

check.note: The quote is verbatim in Section 13 (p. 60). The executive summary says the mean CACC time gap was 45 % of the gap selected with ACC.

claims.quantity: Desired headway assumed for manual driving in the PATH ACC/CACC capacity simulation
claims.value: 1.64 s (≈3600/2200), drawn uniformly within ±10 % (1.48-1.8 s). This is a simulation assumption, not a measurement
claims.source: Shladover, Lu, Nowakowski, Su (2011). Caltrans CA11-2138
claims.quote: we assume the desired headway for manual driving is 1.64 sec (≈3600/2200)

check.corrected_value: 1.64 s desired HEADWAY (gross, front-to-front; ≈3600/2200 for 2200 veh/h). The gap for manual driving is 'selected randomly ... within a +/- 10% error range' (1.48-1.8 s). The report does not say the draw is uniform. This is a simulation assumption used for vehicle entry.

groups.notes:
I read every claim above in this session. The headings below are about how to map the sources onto SUMO, which matters for this group.

(1) Gap vs headway. In SUMO Krauss, tau works on the NET gap, from the leader's back to the follower's front (SUMO docs). These sources report net time gaps and map directly onto tau: Al-Obaedi (UK 'gap headway'), Nishinari/Treiber/Helbing (A9 'netto time gap'), Loulizi (rear-to-front time gap), ISO 15622 (τ = c/v) and UN R157. These sources use GROSS front-to-front headway and need the vehicle-length term removed: Knospe (A3/A1 time-headway), highD lane-change THW, Waymo 'time headway', and probably openACC (I did not check openACC's exact definition). Gunter (s = η + th·v) and Shi & Li (spacing = l + Δ + τ·v) are linear constant-time-gap fits. Their th or τ is closest to tau, and η or Δ is closest to minGap. A Krauss vehicle with tau = th will not reproduce the same equilibrium exactly. For Krauss, minGap is also added to the safe gap (a SUMO detail I did not re-verify here).

(2) Filters and pooling. The UK loop numbers (mean ≈1.1 s, SD ≈0.42 s) are truncated at 2 s and at a speed difference of 1.5 m/s. They describe close following, which is the regime relevant at a bottleneck, not the full desired-gap distribution. The A9 numbers show that the most probable net gap rises from about 0.75 s in free flow to 1.2-1.9 s upstream of bottlenecks (the 'frustration effect'). Gaps are therefore density- and location-dependent; one fixed tau distribution may not hold.

(3) Car vs truck. The evidence conflicts. A9 and highD say truck followers keep larger gaps. In the UK close-following sample, HGVs and cars differ by < 0.1 s at the 70th percentile. In Germany, trucks > 3.5 t must keep 50 m on the Autobahn above 50 km/h. My arithmetic: 50 m is ≈2.25 s at 80 km/h and ≈2.0 s at 90 km/h. This is a legal floor, and compliance is unknown.

(4) CAV. Commercial ACC minimum settings cluster around 0.9-1.5 s: Italy/Sweden openACC peaks 0.9-1.5 s, US model fits 0.54-1.13 s, Lincoln τ 0.83 s. Maximum settings are 1.7-3.5 s. ISO 15622 requires τmin ≥ 0.8 s and at least one setting in 1.5-2.2 s. Choice of setting: in US field data, ACC drivers chose 1.1 s 50.4 % of the time, and CACC drivers chose 0.6 s 57 % of the time. Truck CACC drivers mostly used 1.2 s. The ENSEMBLE truck-platoon floor is > 0.8 s (Level A). UN R157 gives 1.0-1.6 s for cars and 1.2-2.4 s for heavy vehicles up to 60 km/h only.

(5) Region gaps. European HDV standstill-gap (minGap) evidence is missing; only US sources (NGSIM jam spacing 5-9 m including length; queue gap ≈3.66 m) were found.

(6) Access and tags. All values are tagged with the access level actually achieved. Two HDV claims are secondary citations, marked 'review' with VERIFY: Taieb-Maimon & Shinar via Loulizi, and Brackstone et al. via Al-Obaedi. WebFetch-read pages (Highway Code, StVO, the Ford manual, SUMO docs) are tagged FT. Their quotes came through the fetch tool's extraction, so a manual re-check is advisable.

claims.region: n/a (assumption derived from a Netherlands simulator study)

claims.locator: Sec. V, paragraph before Fig. 11; ref. [57]

check.note: Sec. V: 'stricter limits ... Jmin = -1 m/s3, Jmax = 1 m/s3, and amin = -1.25 m/s2, amax = 1.25 m/s2, based on findings from [57]'. [57] is de Winkel, Irmak, Happee, Shyrokau, Applied Ergonomics 106, 103881, 2023. These are the authors' modelling assumption.

gaps: ISO 15622:2018 and ISO 22179:2009 primary texts not read (paywalled). The official iTeh sample of ISO 15622:2018 stops before the operating-limits clause. The speed-dependent limits often attributed to the 2018 edition (acceleration about 4 to 2 m/s2, deceleration 5 to 3.5 m/s2, jerk 5 to 2.5 m/s3 between about 5 and 20 m/s) are only partly backed by what I read: the deceleration range comes from Tordeux 2020; the acceleration and jerk endpoints are unconfirmed. A copy of the 1999 ISO/DIS 15622 on a personal website was found but not downloaded (the permission classifier blocked it), so it was not used.

ISO 22179 (FSRA) numbers: Bernsteiner 2016 (TU Graz thesis, p. 20, Fig. 2.12) shows a speed-dependent maximum deceleration with axis ticks of -3.5 and -5 m/s2, but the figure values could not be read, so they are not claimed.

CACC: no measured or specified acceleration/deceleration limits found. The Milanés & Shladover 2014 (TR-C) full text is blocked on HAL and CORE by anti-bot pages. TNO/Ploeg CACC, ENSEMBLE truck-platooning D2.4/D2.14 and Knoop et al. 2019 (Level-2 platoon, NL) full texts were not read.

European measured commercial ACC acceleration limits: the openACC paper (Makridis et al. 2021, JRC) reports no acceleration-limit numbers. They would have to be computed from the openACC trajectories. Measured ACC data claimed here are US-only (Goodall & Lan; Zhou et al.).

HDV trucks: no European naturalistic distribution found for truck maximum acceleration, comfortable deceleration or emergency deceleration. The highD per-track maxima/minima by class are only in figures (Kruber Fig. 22). Yang et al. 2016 (IJTST, truck acceleration at metered on-ramps, US) is blocked by a captcha. The MDPI 2023 tractor-semitrailer braking paper and the NHTSA heavy-vehicle AEB field study (DOT HS 812 280) are blocked (403). The FMVSS 121 equivalent (0.41 g from 60 mph) is seen only in a search snippet and not used.
Current UN R13 (11 series) N3 value not read. The 5.0 m/s2 figure is from the 1996 Revision 3, and its column assignment was read from extracted layout.

European queue-discharge (start-up) acceleration from field data: not found. Only the US historical review (Long 2000, Table 2) is used. Bokare & Maurya 2017 (India, TR Procedia, per-type max acceleration) is blocked by a captcha. Its values (e.g. 2.23 / 2.87 m/s2 for diesel / petrol cars, 1.0 for trucks) appeared only in a secondary search snippet and are not claimed.

European naturalistic maximum acceleration of cars as a distribution (per driver or per vehicle): not found. Bosetti, Da Lio & Saroldi 2014 (ETRR, Italy) is blocked by a JavaScript challenge. UDRIVE and euroFOT were not searched.

de Winkel et al. 2023 comfort models (Applied Ergonomics): full text not reachable (TU Delft repository timeout; Elsevier 403). Only used via Hadjigeorgiou's paraphrase. Bellem et al. 2018 (TR-F) values not read.
SHRP2/100-car peak deceleration in near-crashes (median 0.74 g) and the AASHTO/NCHRP 400 primary text (Fambro et al.) were seen only in snippets or secondary sources and are not claimed separately.
Jerk for HDV in naturalistic motorway data: only the single chauffeur test-track measurement (Horn 2024). No distribution.
The web search budget ran out near the end of this session. Truck naturalistic deceleration and CACC limits could not be searched further.
groups.notes:
I read 33 claims from 20 distinct sources. All are tagged FT because I read the relevant section or table text myself (via pdftotext or the page itself). Three standards claims (ISO 15622) are standards values quoted by secondary papers. Their access tag refers to the secondary paper, and the primary ISO text was not read.

Arithmetic below is mine, not the sources'. Please verify it.
(1) The highD logistic scale s converts to an SD of s*pi/sqrt(3): about 0.30 m/s2 for cars and 0.13 m/s2 for trucks. These are per-frame accelerations, not per-vehicle maxima.
(2) 0.343 g is about 3.36 m/s2. 0.774 G is about 7.6 m/s2.
(3) The ICCT EU tractor power of 250-380 kW at 40 t gives about 6.3-9.5 kW/t. At the VECTO long-haul mass (14.4 t curb + 19.3 t payload = 33.7 t) it gives about 7.4-11.3 kW/t. The German legal minimum is 5.0 kW/t.
(4) The Zhou et al. ACC acceleration limit at 100 km/h (27.8 m/s) is 0.4 + 12.2*0.015, about 0.58 m/s2. The Goodall Audi Q7 measured 0.57 m/s2 at 90 km/h, which is consistent.

Interpretation for SUMO (hypotheses, not results):
- SUMO docs say accel/decel are 'convenient' values, not maxima.
- European naturalistic braking (EUSight) puts about 95% of braking time at 1-3 m/s2 and treats 3-4 m/s2 as the comfortable bound. This suggests a car decel distribution centred around 3-4 m/s2, below the 4.5 default.
- emergencyDecel for cars can be sourced from the Greibe trials: 7.4 (non-professional) to 8.4 (professional) m/s2 on dry roads, with UN R13-H 6.43 m/s2 as the type-approval floor.
- For trucks, only regulation floors (5.0 m/s2, old R13 text) and a wet-curve experiment (0.16-0.27 g) were found. Truck decel/emergencyDecel would therefore be partly an assumption.
- For CAV-ACC, ISO 15622 (2.0 accel / 3.5 decel / 2.5 jerk) and openpilot clips (2.0 / -3.5) agree. Measured production ACC accelerates up to about 2.7 m/s2 at low speed but only about 0.6 m/s2 near 90-100 km/h, and rarely brakes harder than 2 m/s2.
- Automated-driving comfort studies point to about 1.0-1.5 m/s2 deceleration and jerk of about 0.3-1.0 m/s3.
- UN R157 sets >5 m/s2 as the emergency boundary and 4 m/s2 as the MRM target.

Caveats:
- Krauss uses decel inside its safe-speed rule, so lowering it changes gap acceptance and capacity, not only braking. I am fairly but not fully sure of this for SUMO 1.27; check the SUMO car-following docs.
- SUMO's Krauss has no jerk limit. I did not verify in this session which SUMO models (e.g. EIDM) expose jerk parameters.
- Region labels: Long 2000, MPC 17-338, Goodall and Zhou are US data. The R157 human-model values come from Japan/NHTSA experiments.

I read only the abstract, not the full text.

claims.quantity: HDV brake onset timing relative to kinematic urgency (looming threshold) in naturalistic rear-end crashes and near-crashes; cars, heavy trucks, buses
claims.sumo_param: actionStepLength (proxy); also relevant to driverstate perception thresholds
claims.value: Eyes-off-threat events: brake onset within 1 s of first looming tau^-1 >= 0.2 s^-1 in 141/142 (99 %), mean 0.42 s after it. Eyes-on-threat: 80/122 (66 %) within 1 s, 16 % before the threshold, 18 % more than 1 s after. 323 events after exclusions (99 crashes: 62 car, 37 truck/bus; 224 near-crashes: 210 car, 14 truck/bus)
claims.region: US (SHRP 2) plus ANNEXT (Lytx-recorded; region not checked)
claims.source: Markkula, G., Engström, J., Lodin, J., Bärgman, J., Victor, T. (2016). A farewell to brake reaction times? Kinematics-dependent brake response in naturalistic rear-end emergencies. Accident Analysis & Prevention (author postprint)
claims.quote: Of the 142 eyes-off-threat events in Figure 6, brake onset came within one second after t0.2 in 141 cases (99 %), and the average was 0.42 s after t0.2.

check.note: Sec. 5.2 has the 1-1.5 s quote, no correlation with target speed, and 152 of 340 partial trajectories discarded (correlation threshold 0.7). The abstract gives 30-60 km/h. The dynamic-platform tests reached only 30 and 40 km/h. Site: ZalaZONE, Hungary.

claims.quantity: Commercial ACC string stability vs time-gap setting (measured)
claims.value: Short gap: perturbation magnitude more than doubled from 2nd to last vehicle (string unstable). Long gap: median weak-stability indicator at last vehicle about 0.5 (attenuated). Medium gap: roughly neutral. 33 perturbations, 10 vehicles, 30-40 km/h
claims.source: Ciuffo, B., et al. (2021). Requiem on the positive effects of commercial adaptive cruise control... Transportation Research Part C 130, 103305
claims.quote: for the shortest time gap setting, the magnitude of the perturbation has more than doubled, moving from the second vehicle to the last in the platoon

check.note: Sec. 5.3/5.3.1 give 33 perturbations and 10 vehicles. The short gap 'more than doubled' from the 2nd to the last vehicle. The long-gap median indicator for the last vehicle is close to 0.5. For the medium gap the indicator 'remains fairly constant' (only slowly attenuated). Speeds were 30 and 40 km/h.

claims.quantity: String instability of SAE level-2 (ACC + lane centering) platoon on public roads
claims.value: 7 vehicles, almost 500 km; unsuitable for platoons of more than about 3-4 vehicles
claims.source: Knoop, V. L., Wang, M., Wilmink, I. R., Hoedemaeker, D. M., Maaskant, M., Van der Meer, E.-J. (2019). Platoon of SAE Level-2 Automated Vehicles on Public Roads: Setup, Traffic Interactions, and Stability. Transportation Research Record
claims.quote: the current SAE level-2 systems are not suitable for driving as platoons of more than typically three to four vehicles, because of instabilities in the car-following behavior

check.note: The OpenAlex abstract (TRR 2673(9):311-322) has seven SAE level-2 vehicles, almost 500 km, and the quote exactly. I read only the abstract.

claims.quantity: ACC time-gap range in ISO 15622:2018 (secondary citation) and review verdict on commercial ACC stability
claims.value: ISO 15622 time gap 0.8 to 2.2 s (as cited); ADAC guideline 1.8 s; the review concludes commercial ACC is not string stable because of high response times
claims.region: international standard (cited in a German review)
claims.source: Korbmacher, R., Khound, P., Tordeux, A. (2025). Understanding Collective Stability of ACC Systems: From Theory to Real-World Observations. arXiv:2504.04530 (citing ISO 15622:2018)
claims.quote: It is also the strategy recommended by safety standards such as ISO 15622, with a time gap ranging from 0.8 to 2.2 seconds [7]

check.note: The introduction has the quote with ref [7] = ISO 15622:2018 and gives 1.8 s for the German ADAC guidelines. The abstract says commercial ACC is not string stable because of high response times. This is a secondary citation; I did not check the ISO text.

claims.quantity: Measured V2V one-way latency for CACC: ITS-G5 (802.11p) vs LTE PC5
claims.value: ITS-G5: mode about 4 ms, mean 3.4-3.9 ms, SD 1-1.5 ms, >95 % within 5 ms, PER < 0.1 % (iCLCM) and < 0.02 % (CAM). LTE PC5: mode 22-25 ms, mean 38 ms, SD 13-15 ms, values up to 80 ms, PER 4.5-5 %. LTE Uu penalty about 50 ms. CAM/iCLCM at 25 Hz. Two Toyota Prius, no-traffic test track
claims.source: Cimoli, B., Xing, H., Ho, V., Passchier, I., Kakes, G., Rommel, S., Nijmeijer, H., Tafur Monroy, I. (2022). Practical Challenges in Hybrid Communication Ecosystems Based on ITS-G5 and LTE for CACC and GLOSA. Frontiers in Future Transportation
claims.quote: the mean drops between 3.4 and 3.9 ms and the standard deviation is between 1 and 1.5 ms. Moreover, more than 95% of the messages was received within 5 ms.

check.corrected_value: LTE PC5 mean: 38.0 ms for CAM but 30.8 ms for iCLCM (Table 1); 95th percentile 65 ms (CAM) and 56 ms (iCLCM). ITS-G5 SD 1.0 (CAM) and 1.7 ms (iCLCM) in Table 1 (the text says 1-1.5 ms); 95th percentile 4-5 ms.
check.note: The text has the quote, mode 22-25 ms, values up to 80 ms, PC5 PER 4.5-5 %, ITS-G5 PER < 0.1 % (iCLCM) and < 0.02 % (CAM), 25 Hz, two Toyota Prius at RDW Lelystad with no traffic. The abstract gives a PC5/Uu penalty of 20/50 ms. The 38 ms mean holds only for CAMs.

claims.quantity: CACC string-stable settings: maximum tolerable communication delay vs time gap; identified vehicle lag
claims.sumo_param: none (CACC tau = time gap for context)
claims.value: Vehicle parameters (identified in Ploeg et al. 2011): τ = 0.1 s, actuator delay θa = 0.2 s. Time gaps 0.3 / 0.6 / 1.0 s tolerate at most 29 / 111 / 300 ms delay (constant latency, no packet loss)
claims.source: Cimoli, B., et al. (2022). Frontiers in Future Transportation (theoretical analysis citing Xing et al. 2019 and Ploeg et al. 2011)
claims.quote: time gaps of 0.3, 0.6, and 1.0 s require maximum delays of 29 ms, 111 ms, and 300 ms, respectively

check.note: Sec. 2: 'The vehicle parameters have been identified in (Ploeg et al., 2011): τ = 0.1, θa = 0.2 s'. Time gaps 0.3/0.6/1.0 s tolerate at most 29/111/300 ms. The analysis assumes constant latency and ignores packet loss (Xing et al. 2019).

claims.quantity: CACC fallback to ACC on communication loss (field prototype)
claims.sumo_param: none (SUMO CACC has its own ACC fallback logic)
claims.value: Degrades to ACC after 3 lost packets or latency > 100 ms; at 0.3 s time gap all three links (ITS-G5, PC5, Uu) still gave string-stable platoon behaviour
claims.source: Cimoli, B., et al. (2022). Frontiers in Future Transportation
claims.quote: the CACC will degrade to ACC mode when three packets are lost or the latency of over 100 ms due to the safety functionality

check.corrected_value: The fallback is confirmed: CACC degrades to ACC after 3 lost packets or latency > 100 ms. String stability at h = 0.3 s is claimed for all three links only in the abstract. The body and conclusion support it for ITS-G5 and LTE PC5. For LTE Uu with TLS on, Table 2 shows the follower decelerating at 1.68 m/s² against the leader's 1.57 m/s² ('the deceleration is amplified'), and latencies above 100 ms caused fluctuations. The platoon had only 2 vehicles (P2 leading P3).
check.note: The quote is in the text. The claim that Uu was also string stable rests only on the abstract and is contradicted by the Table 2 Uu TLS-on row.

gaps: The web-search budget ran out (200 calls per turn, shared by all agents), so the items below were not searched further. A follow-up message can resume the search.
Johansson & Rumar (1971) brake reaction times: not verified in any source read here.
Ma & Andréasson (Sweden) car-following reaction-time distribution (reported as lognormal): parameters not obtained.
No truck-specific brake-reaction-time distribution found. The only truck values are Hoogendoorn & Ossen (2006, NL, n=65) for car-following and the pooled truck/bus events in Markkula et al. (2016).
No Europe-specific naturalistic brake reaction times (e.g., UDRIVE) found. Region of the Dozza (2013) row in the TRB table not verified.
The TRB table lists Sivak et al. 1982 (N=1,644; mean 1.21 s). Taoka (1989) lists Sivak et al. 1981 (87 drivers; mean 1.38 s). They look like different data sets; not reconciled.

Krauss sigma calibrated on European motorway trajectories (highD, etc.): none found. The only per-vehicle sigma/actionStepLength distributions are from a US urban signalized arterial (Schrader et al. 2024).

European speed-holding fluctuation data (SD of speed or acceleration noise in free flow on motorways) and the Guensler/Ko Atlanta acceleration-noise values: not obtained. Laval et al. (2014) random-acceleration parameter: not searched (budget).
Peter Wagner (2022, SUMO conference, simTD Germany) action-point time distribution: the full paper read here gives no numeric inter-action-point statistics.

Milanés & Shladover (2014) full text was blocked (HAL bot check, CORE Cloudflare). Its ACC/CACC time gaps (commonly cited as 1.1 s and 0.6 s) and first-order lag values were not verified. Only the SUMO defaults derived from it are reported.
Ploeg et al. (2011) full text not read; τ = 0.1 s and θa = 0.2 s are taken from Cimoli et al. (2022).
ISO 15622:2018 and UN R157 texts not read directly; values come from secondary sources (Korbmacher et al. 2025; Olleja et al. 2025).
ETSI EN 302 637-2 CAM generation intervals (100 ms to 1 s) and SAE J2945/1 BSM 10 Hz: not verified.

Commercial ACC actuation lag as a first-order time constant (rather than a delay fitted in Gunter's model or the correlation-based response time) not found. Li et al. (2021, TR-B) and Shi & Li (2021, TR-C) could not be accessed.
Automated-driving prototype (e.g., Waymo) sensing-to-actuation lag or response time: no usable source found.
Truck ACC/CACC actuation lag from field data: not found. Only simulation assumptions (Salek et al.) and PATH truck time-gap settings.
The SUMO documentation pages read are the current online versions (some edited 2026). They should be checked against the 1.27.1 docs/source before relying on defaults.
groups.notes:
Coverage: 36 claims. HDV reaction time: 11 claims (brake RT expected/unexpected, naturalistic SHRP 2, lognormal fit, NL motorway car-following Tr for cars vs trucks, action-point intervals, R157 benchmark). HDV speed fluctuation: 7 claims (Krauss sigma calibration distribution, SUMO sigma/driverstate/EIDM/HDM parameters, acceleration noise, platoon oscillation growth). CAV: 18 claims (ACC delay and response times, measured string instability, CACC latency and string-stable delay limits, 3GPP requirements, SUMO ACC/CACC gains, truck CACC gaps and lags).

Key interpretation cautions, which are my inferences, not source statements:
(1) Several quantities are called "reaction time" but are not the same thing.
- Brake reaction time to an unexpected event: means about 1.1-1.5 s, roughly lognormal, SD 0.4-1.0 s, P90 about 2.2 s in SHRP 2.
- Car-following stimulus-response delay Tr: about 1.4-1.5 s on the NL A15, trucks about the same as cars.
- Action-point interval: mean about 2.5 s.
- SUMO actionStepLength: per-vehicle calibration P50 0.3-0.4 s, on a US arterial only.
- None of these maps one-to-one onto actionStepLength. SUMO's own note says the action step is not a true reaction delay. Krauss tau is a desired headway, not a reaction time.
(2) For ACC, the correlation-based "response time" (JRC: 1-2.6 s; Makridis 2020: 0.8-1.2 s) and Gunter's fitted delay τ (0.15-0.99 s) are defined differently. Do not pool them.
(3) A search snippet attributed "1.7-2.5 s" to Makridis et al. 2020. The abstract retrieved from OpenAlex says 0.8-1.2 s. The 1.6-2.6 s range matches openACC Table IV instead.
(4) Evidence on measured string stability is consistent: commercial ACC is unstable at short gaps (US: 7 of 7 models; EU: ZalaZONE, AstaZero, NL L2 platoon). Long gaps attenuate perturbations in the ZalaZONE data.
(5) CACC string stability depends on the time gap and on latency. With τ = 0.1 s and θa = 0.2 s, a 0.3 s gap tolerates only about 29 ms. Measured ITS-G5 latency (about 4 ms) fits within that, while LTE PC5 (mean 38 ms) does not at 0.3 s under that constant-delay analysis. The field tests still reported string-stable behaviour at 0.3 s.
(6) The SUMO docs say the driver-state device supports Krauss, IDM, ACC and CACC. This resolves the earlier uncertainty, but should be confirmed for 1.27.1.
(7) The Schrader table header says P95 while the text describes 10th/50th/90th percentiles. Treat the upper value as P90 or P95 (unclear).

groups.title: Lane changing and merging

claims.quantity: Accepted gap / post-encroachment time (PET) of on-ramp merges onto the motorway
claims.value: n=137 correctly extracted merges. Merging behind a mainline vehicle: median PET 4.0 s, 25th percentile 2.6 s. Merging in front of a mainline vehicle: median 3.0 s, 25th percentile 2.0 s. Merging into a gap (sum of PETs, i.e. accepted gap): roughly uniform on [5.0, 15.1] s, mean 9.7 ± 2.9 s
claims.region: Germany (A39 near Cremlingen, Test Bed Lower Saxony)
claims.source: Klitzke L., Gimm K., Koch C., Köster F., 'Extraction and Analysis of Highway On-Ramp Merging Scenarios from Naturalistic Trajectory Data', arXiv:2104.05661v2 (2022)
claims.quote: with 50% having a PET lower than 4.0 seconds and 25% lower than 2.6 seconds. For the into type the PET is uniformly distributed within [5.0; 15.1] seconds and a mean of 9.7 ± 2.9 seconds

check.note: arXiv:2104.05661v2, Sec. IV-B/C with Fig. 10: 137 of 144 merges extracted correctly; behind: 50% < 4.0 s, 25% < 2.6 s; in front: 50% < 3.0 s, 25% < 2.0 s; into (sum of PETs, 'related to the SMoS accepted gap time'): uniform on [5.0; 15.1] s, mean 9.7 ± 2.9 s. The 137 count covers all categories, including 'free'.

claims.quantity: Critical net time gap to the target-lane follower (Raff's method), by lane-change objective
claims.value: Cooperative lane changes: critical gap 0.68 s. Lane changes made right after merging from an on-ramp (merging/overtaking): critical gap 0.9 s. Time gaps above 5 s were excluded. Rejected-gap sample too small for lane changes to the right
claims.source: Hofinger F., Fellendorf M., 'Lane change behavior on motorways based on naturalistic trajectory data', hEART 2023 conference paper 2329
claims.quote: The accepted gaps as well as the critical gap of 0.68s for cooperative lane changes is rather low. ... Figure 3c shows a criti- cal gap of 0.9s for lane changes, which are performed immediately after conducting a merging lane change from an on-ramp.

check.note: Sec. 3: net time gap to the target-lane follower, gaps > 5 s excluded; critical gap 0.68 s (cooperative) and 0.9 s (lane change right after an on-ramp merge); no rejected-gap distribution for right lane changes because too few cases were observed. Authors are at TU Graz.

claims.quantity: Time headway (THW) at cut-in manoeuvres
claims.value: 850 cut-ins; THW from about 0.1 to 4 s, distribution peak at 1 s
claims.source: Kruber F., Wurst J., Chakraborty S., Botsch M., 'Highway traffic data: macroscopic, microscopic and criticality analysis for capturing relevant traffic scenarios and traffic modeling based on the highD data set', arXiv:1903.04249 (2019); key facts adopted from Krajewski et al. 2018 (highD paper)
claims.locator: Section II, bulleted key facts of the highD data set
claims.quote: 850 cut-in maneuvers: THW from around 0.1 - 4 s with a distribution peak at 1 s

check.note: Text matches verbatim: '850 cut-in maneuvers: THW from around 0.1 - 4 s with a distribution peak at 1 s', adopted from Krajewski et al. The locator is wrong: the list is in Section IV ('highD data set'), not Section II.

claims.quantity: Critical time gaps for mandatory lane changes (gamma-distributed), lead and lag
claims.value: Combined data: mean lead critical gap 1.17 s (variance 0.82 s²), mean lag critical gap 1.26 s (variance 0.87 s²). Gamma parameters (alpha, beta), Table 6: uncongested, adjacent to shoulder lane: lead 1.54/0.80, lag 2.42/0.47; shoulder to adjacent lane: lead 1.49/0.61, lag 1.10/0.92. Congested, adjacent to shoulder: lead 1.88/0.71, lag 1.98/0.71; shoulder to adjacent: lead 1.78/0.66, lag 1.57/0.79. Lag and lead critical gaps were 22 % and 15 % larger in congestion. About 30 % of drivers were inconsistent (rejected gaps larger than the accepted one). Only gaps ≤ 5 s were analysed
claims.region: USA (NGSIM, I-80 type weaving section with on-/off-ramp)
claims.source: Bham G.H., 'Analyzing Microscopic Behavior: Driver Mandatory Lane Change Behavior on a Multilane Freeway', Report UTC R157, Missouri University of Science & Technology, August 2008
claims.locator: p. 11 (Maximum Likelihood Estimation) and Table 6 (Gamma Distribution Parameters for Critical Gaps)
claims.quote: Mean leading and trailing critical gaps for the combined datasets (uncongested and congested) and for the both the lane change maneuvers combined, were found to be 1.17 and 1.26 seconds, and the variance to be 0.82 and 0.87 seconds2, respectively.

check.note: Read the PDF through WebFetch because curl got 403. p. 11: means 1.17/1.26 s, variances 0.82/0.87 s². Table 6 values match exactly. Trailing 22% and leading 15% larger in congestion; about 30% inconsistent drivers; only gaps ≤ 5 s used. Site: NGSIM I-80, Emeryville CA (2004/2005).

claims.quantity: Accepted time gaps in mandatory lane changes, and how they shrink near a lane drop (urgency or impatience)
claims.value: Mean accepted gap 1.34 s; mean of median accepted gaps 1.13 s (uncongested 1.29 s, congested 1.40 s). Accepted gaps get shorter as drivers approach the lane drop / off-ramp
claims.source: Bham G.H., 'Analyzing Microscopic Behavior: Driver Mandatory Lane Change Behavior on a Multilane Freeway', Report UTC R157, Missouri University of Science & Technology, August 2008
claims.locator: Accepted Gaps section (Table 2 discussion); Critical Gaps section, p. 10
claims.quote: The mean value of accepted gaps was found to be 1.34 secs and the mean value of the median accepted gaps was found to be 1.13 secs. ... As the drivers approach the off-ramp when traveling on the shoulder lane, the accepted gaps get shorter as the drivers approached the lane drop.

check.corrected_value: Mean accepted gap 1.34 s; mean of median accepted gaps 1.13 s. The 1.29 s (uncongested) and 1.40 s (congested) are MEAN accepted gaps. The median was 1.13 s in both data sets. The shorter gaps near the lane drop are offered as a qualitative explanation for the larger congested critical gaps, not as a measured result.
check.note: The numbers are present, but the parenthetical attaches the uncongested/congested split to the median, which the source contradicts ('Differences were not observed in the median values ... 1.13 secs for the two field data sets').

claims.quantity: Lead and lag time gaps in discretionary lane changes on a freeway
claims.value: n=477 discretionary lane changes; median lead gap 1.72 s, median lag gap 1.91 s; heavy-tailed, lognormal preferred over power law. Mean lag relative speed 1.43 m/s, mean lead relative speed -0.35 m/s

claims.quote: The median • Lead gap: 1.72 sec • Lag gap: 1.91 sec ... Results show the gaps are more likely to be Log- normal distributed

Mean relative speeds: lead -0.35, lag 1.43 m/s. The slides do not say 'Chicago' (I-294 is in the Chicago area from general knowledge).

claims.value: About 1 lane change per veh-km in very light traffic, falling to about 0.5 per veh-km at densities near capacity. The count rises sharply with density and starts to fall at about 25 veh/km

'The number of lane changes increases sharply with the density, but the number starts to decrease at around 25 veh/km' (the absolute count; the text does not say whether this density is per lane).

claims.quantity: Lane-change counts in the highD dataset (basis for a per-veh-km rate)
claims.value: About 110,500 vehicles, 45,000 km driven in total, 11,000 lane changes (5,600 completed inside the observed area); 77 % cars, 23 % trucks. At lane crossing, lead gaps exceed about 0.54 s and lag gaps about 0.65 s; lag gap is usually larger than lead gap. Near-leader group: median lead gap rose from -0.24 s at activation to 0.75 s at crossing; another group's median lag gap rose from 0.41 s to 0.85 s. Target-lane platoon at about 40 mph (limit 45 mph)
claims.region: USA (Sunset Lake Road, Apex, North Carolina; summer 2025)
claims.source: Sharma A., Al Hasan M.A., Chen D., List G.F., 'Controlled Experiments on Lane Changing by Transitional Autonomous Vehicle: Dataset and Behavioral Insights', arXiv:2607.27085v2 (Aug 2026)
claims.locator: Experiment design section; 'Gap acceptance and evolution' section, Figs. 5-7
claims.quote: at LCC, the lead and lag gaps exceed approximately 0.54 s and 0.65 s, respectively, and the lag gap is larger than the lead gap in most cases.

check.note: Sunset Lake Rd, Apex NC, summer 2025; right-turn lanes 173 m (NB) / 169 m (SB); 78 trials; platoon stabilised at 40 mph, limit 45 mph. At LC crossing: lead > about 0.54 s, lag > about 0.65 s, lag usually larger. Near-leader median lead gap -0.24 to 0.75 s; near-follower median lag gap 0.41 to 0.85 s.

claims.quantity: Cooperative merge into a CACC platoon (field experiment): headway taken by the merging vehicle and merge time
claims.sumo_param: none directly (CACC vType tau; lcCooperative of platoon vehicles)
claims.value: Merge-vehicle headway to its new leader 0.5-1.5 s (mostly near 1.5 s); intraplatoon headway 0.84 s measured. Mean time to merge Tm: 35 s automated vs 36 s manual (no significant difference; set mainly by geometry). The authors estimate a 7 % merge-area capacity loss (3,973 to 3,703 veh/h/lane) for a 10-vehicle platoon
claims.region: USA (I-95 express lanes, Virginia; managed lane)
claims.source: FHWA, 'Applying Bundled Speed-Harmonization, Cooperative Adaptive Cruise Control, and Cooperative-Merge Applications to Managed-Lane Facilities', FHWA-HRT-21-008, March 2021
claims.locator: Chapter 4, Merging Analysis pp. 84-89; capacity analysis p. 95-96 (Table 16)
claims.quote: the actual headway between the merge vehicle and the fourth vehicle (the merge vehicle is fifth) actually varies from 0.5 to 1.5 s (mostly at the higher end).

check.note: Merge-vehicle headway 0.5-1.5 s (mostly at the higher end), verbatim. Intraplatoon headway 0.84 s (also the desired CACC headway). Tm 35 s automated vs 36 s manual; the 'no significant difference' is judged from averages, not a stated test. Capacity 3,973 to 3,703 veh/h/lane, 7% (Table 16: 6.8%, 10-vehicle platoon). I-95 express lanes, Virginia.

claims.quantity: Effect of connected cooperative-merge speed guidance on minimum headway at a ramp merge (driving-simulator experiment)
claims.value: Median minimum time headway, non-guided vs guided: mainline car 0.75 vs 1.76 s; ramp car 0.73 vs 0.74 s; mainline truck 1.11 vs 1.11 s; ramp truck 1.04 vs 1.03 s. The report labels the mainline-car change '+57%', which does not match 0.75 to 1.76 (about +135 %). 7 volunteer car drivers plus one researcher in the truck simulator; human drivers given V2X speed advice
claims.source: METRANS report PSR-21-20, 'Connectivity-Based Cooperative Ramp Merging in Multimodal and Mixed Traffic Environment' (final report, revised)
claims.quote: Mainline Car 0.75 1.76 +57%

check.note: Table 5, p. 35, matches: 1.11/1.11, 1.04/1.03, 0.75/1.76 (+57%), 0.73/0.74 (+4%). The +57% equals (1.76-0.75)/1.76, i.e. relative to the guided value; as a conventional increase it would be about +135%. The ramp-car +4% fits neither base. 7 volunteers drove the car simulator; one person drove the truck simulator in all runs. Report PSR-21-20, UC Riverside, Sept 2022.

gaps: Daamen, Loot & Hoogendoorn (2010), 'Empirical analysis of merging behavior at freeway on-ramp', TRR 2188 (Netherlands): exists, but I could not access its accepted-gap or merge-position values.
Marczak, Daamen & Buisson (2013), ISTTT/Procedia 80 and TR-C (Netherlands + France merges): HAL full text blocked by bot protection, and the TU Delft page had no abstract. No numbers obtained.
Toledo & Zohar (2007), 'Modeling duration of lane changes', TRR 1999 (NGSIM, lognormal): only the bibliographic record seen. Mean and distribution parameters not obtained.
Lee (2006) MIT thesis on freeway merge gap acceptance (critical gap function): the core.ac.uk download returned HTML. Not read.
Truck vs car accepted lead/lag gaps (Aghabayk et al. TRR 2260; Moridpour et al.; Li, Ma & Yang TRR 2676 on 433 highD heavy-vehicle DLCs): not read, so no truck gap-acceptance values from Europe.
European share of forced (mandatory) vs discretionary lane changes, and their gap differences: not found. A last search could not run because the web-search budget was used up.

Keep-right compliance in Europe (share of vehicles in the left or middle lane at low flow; UK middle-lane hogging): only qualitative highD trends and the secondhand Busch (1984) saturation flows. No compliance rate found.

European zipper-merge compliance or closed-lane utilisation (DE Reißverschluss, NL ritsen): none found. A BASt statement that no data has been collected appeared only in a search snippet and is not used as a claim.
Truck lane-change frequency (per veh-km) and truck lane-change duration outside highD: not found.

lcSpeedGain, lcKeepRight and lcCooperative calibrated against European trajectory data: none found. The only data-based calibrations found are TransAID/Mintsis (lcAssertive vs a Hyundai prototype AV) and Wang et al. (US, macroscopic, non-unique).
Manufacturer specifications of automated lane-change gap thresholds (Tesla, BMW, Mercedes, GM Super Cruise, Ford BlueCruise): not found.
L3Pilot Motorway Chauffeur lane-change gap and time-gap data (deliverables D7.x): only seen in search snippets. Not read.
GCDC 2016 (A270, NL) cooperative merging gap metrics: the PDF download timed out. No numbers.
European field tests of cooperative merging or cooperative lane change with measured gaps (AdaptIVe VW-Volvo 2017, Hi-Drive, IMAGinE, MAVEN, TransAID real-world tests): no quantitative results found.

AV lane changes on freeways: Waymo data used are mainly urban or arterial. Ali et al. (2024) on WOMD (AVs keep larger lead/lag gaps and longer execution times) was seen only as a citation inside Sharma et al. Not read.
Commercial ACC cut-in rates and gaps accepted by humans cutting in front of ACC/CACC strings on European motorways: not found (the TNO EcoTwin report excerpt had no cut-in counts).
Commonly cited rules of thumb (e.g. a critical merge gap of about 1 s, HCM gap values, highD lane-change counts by lane) were not checked against a primary source and are not reported.
groups.notes:
Mapping to SUMO and caveats:
(1) Gap acceptance to lcAssertive. Per the SUMO docs (fetched 2026-10-28; the docs track the current release, so check against 1.27.1), lcAssertive is the "Willingness to accept lower front and rear gaps on the target lane. The required gap is divided by this value." LC2013's required gap comes from braking-based safe gaps, not a time gap. So the time-gap data above (HDV critical gaps 0.68-0.9 s in highD/exiD; 1.17/1.26 s in NGSIM MLC; median DLC lead/lag 1.72/1.91 s on I-24; cut-in THW peak 1 s in highD) map to lcAssertive only through a simulation check. That is how TransAID matched lcAssertive to Hyundai prototype data: CAV about 0.85, legacy vehicles about 1.2, with 1.3 judged too aggressive. The regulatory CAV rules (R157: 3.0 m/s² after 0.4/1.4 s, 1.0 s residual gap; R79: a=3 m/s², tB=0.4 s, tG=1 s) suggest CAV lcAssertive ≤ 1. That is my inference, not a sourced calibration.
(2) lcImpatience and lcTimeToImpatience are listed in the SUMO docs as SL2015-only. If that holds for 1.27.1, the earlier assistant table that listed lcImpatience under LC2013 is wrong. Under LC2013, urgency near a lane end goes through lcStrategic and lcLookaheadLeft. Bham found accepted gaps shrink near the lane drop. Please verify this in the 1.27.1 source or docs before relying on it.
(3) Lane-change duration maps to --lanechange.duration (global, seconds) or per-vType maxSpeedLat, which overrides the duration. Two highD studies disagree: car means of 5.7 s (Li, Li & Ni) vs 7.6-7.8 s (Li, Yang & Pan), because they define start and end differently. Trucks run about 0.5-0.9 s longer. My arithmetic, not sourced: a 3.5 m lane in 5.7-7.6 s is a lateral speed of about 0.46-0.61 m/s; R79 requires the LCM in < 5 s for M1/N1 and < 10 s for N2/N3.
(4) Lane-change frequency targets: UK M42 0.5-1 LC/veh-km; highD about 0.24 LC/veh-km (my arithmetic: 11,000 LCs / 45,000 veh-km); China 0.83-1.04. Guo et al. cite Knoop et al. as 0.4-0.5 per veh-km, but the Knoop paper I read says 1 down to 0.5. They may be citing a different Knoop paper.
(5) Calibration studies: Pelizza et al. (2023) state that Mintsis et al. (TransAID D3.1) is the only real-data SUMO lane-change calibration, and it covers lcAssertive only. Wang et al. (I-24, US) calibrated all five LC2013 parameters on macroscopic data. The results are non-unique (lcAssertive 2.47-4.84; lcKeepRight 0.05-0.56 depending on the measurement type), and some calibrated values exceed the stated bounds (tau 2.56 > 2.0; vf 40.23 > 40). Treat them as weakly identified.
(6) Boukhellouf et al. found that default SUMO merges give only a 1.7-3.8 % capacity drop, against 5-30 % in the field. This is consistent with the project's V145 problem.
(7) The Metrans driving-simulator table contradicts itself: 0.75 to 1.76 s is labelled +57 %.
(8) Waymo-based CAV results are from US urban or arterial roads. The Alhuraish (2026) and Sharma (2026) papers are arXiv preprints and may not be peer-reviewed.
(9) Guo et al. (PLOS ONE) and the StVO text were read through WebFetch extraction of the relevant passages. All other sources were downloaded and read with pdftotext.
(10) Process: background curl jobs saved dot40452.pdf, iowa_zipper.pdf and lee_mit_core4399725.pdf into the repo root by mistake. I moved them to the scratchpad straight away; git status then showed only the pre-existing untracked papers/refs_papers/. Downloads and text extracts are in /tmp/claude-1000/-srv-shared-Workspace-phd-phd-speed-harmo-v5b1/31d6d8e5-e88c-4870-9b77-cc7ccfbaac6c/scratchpad/research/lanechange/.
(11) The web-search budget for this turn ran out before the final search on mandatory vs discretionary lane-change comparisons. A follow-up turn could continue it.

groups.title: Speed choice and speed-limit compliance

claims.quantity: Free-flow speed distribution of cars on motorways (70 mph = 112.7 km/h limit), incl. compliance

claims.quote: Motorways | [no notes] | Percentage of vehicles 65 to 69 miles per hour | 27 ... Percentage of vehicles exceeding speed limit | 44 ... Average free flow speed (miles per hour) | 68

claims.quote: Sattelzug mit Anhänger 2.760 85,5 88,0 2.534 91,8%

claims.quote: Op wegen met een snelheidslimiet tot en met 100 km/u ligt de V85 boven de snelheidslimiet en zelfs op of net boven de verbalisatiegrens.

claims.quote: Der im Abgas-Großversuch für Pkw 1984/85 auf Autobahnen ermittelte Befolgungsgrad einer Geschwindigkeitsbeschränkung auf 120 km/h betrug 63 %, bei einer Geschwindigkeitsbeschränkung auf 100 km/h noch 26 %.

claims.quantity: Compliance with variable mandatory speed limits (managed motorway, M42 ATM pilot)

claims.locator: Section 5.4 Compliance, Figure 5A (figure itself missing from the PDF copy)
claims.quote: the compliance at 70mph to 50mph has remained consistently high, with the compliance at 40mph more variable, but still averaging around 85%.

check.note: Section 5.4 is quoted verbatim. The Figure 5A caption reads 'Monthly compliance on the main carriageway at the ACPO threshold', sourced from HA M42 ATM monitoring of Jan-Feb 2009. The figure's values are not in the extracted text, so the 70-50 mph compliance has no number. The 40 mph variation is attributed to overnight roadworks.

claims.quantity: Compliance with variable advisory speed (VAS, not enforced): distribution of speed minus displayed speed
claims.value: OR 217, one day (18 Mar 2015): mean = median +18 km/h above display, sd 11 km/h; 88 % above, 10 % below; 57 % within +-16 km/h, 15 % within +-8 km/h. 23 weekdays: 80 % faster, 37 % more than 20 % faster. Weekends: 87 % faster, 51 % more than 20 % faster. Drivers ran about 16 km/h above displays of 64-80 km/h; median slightly below display at 48 and 56 km/h

claims.quantity: Mandatory in-vehicle Intelligent Speed Assistance: speed-control band, response and accuracy

claims.quote: (perceived speed limit – 5 km/h) ≤ stabilised speed ≤ perceived speed limit

check.note: Read on the LawPlayer compilation; the direct EUR-Lex fetch returned an empty page. Annex I 3.6.1.1: deceleration <= 3.0 m/s2. 3.6.1.2: intervention within 1.5 s. 3.6.1.3: (perceived limit - 5 km/h) <= stabilised speed <= perceived limit, with speed varying by no more than 4 % or 2 km/h. 3.4.2.5: TP_D >= 90 % of total distance and >= 80 % per road type. Caveats: all speeds are SPEEDOMETER speeds, and speed control is only one of four allowed ISA options.

claims.sumo_param: none (share of drivers with ISA on or overridden)

claims.source: Commission Delegated Regulation (EU) 2021/1958 (intelligent speed assistance), text as compiled by LawPlayer from EUR-Lex
claims.quote: It shall be possible for the driver to override the SCF intervention by performing a positive action.

check.note: Annex I 3.2.1: manual full or partial deactivation. 3.2.1.1: automatically reinstated at each activation of the vehicle master control switch. 3.6.1.4 is quoted verbatim, e.g. pressing the accelerator harder or deeper. Article 4 names the four functions: cascaded acoustic warning, cascaded vibrating warning, haptic feedback, speed control. LawPlayer compilation, not EUR-Lex directly.

claims.quantity: Automated driving (ALKS, SAE L3): maximum speed and obligation to follow speed limits
claims.sumo_param: speedFactor = 1 or below and speedDev = 0 for AV vType; maxSpeed <= 36.1 m/s

claims.locator: Paras 2.1, 5.1.2, 5.2.3.1; Annex test table ('No violation of traffic rules')
claims.quote: The activated system shall comply with traffic rules relating to the DDT in the country of operation, including responding to emergency/enforcement vehicles.

check.note: E/ECE/TRANS/505/Rev.3/Add.156/Amend.4 (3 Mar 2023, 01 series). 2.1: speed of 130 km/h or less. 5.2.3.1: maximum 130 km/h, and above 60 km/h only if an MRM lane change is possible. 5.1.2 is quoted verbatim. The Annex 6 test table has 'Adheres to speed limits' and 'Repeated changes in speed limit above 60 km/h', both mandatory. The regulation does not prescribe speedFactor = 1; that mapping is the claim's own interpretation.

claims.quantity: Speeding while driving with commercial full-range ACC + lane keeping versus manual driving (naturalistic)
claims.value: 7,175 valid 10-s motorway intervals (limits 100/120/130 km/h), 10 drivers, BMW 5 series and Tesla Model S: with a lead vehicle present drivers were speeding 19.3 % of the time (all system states); drivers were less likely to speed with ACC+LKS than in manual baseline. claims.source: Varotto, S.F., Mons, C., Hogema, J.H., Christoph, M., van Nes, N., Martens, M.H. (2022). Do adaptive cruise control and lane keeping systems make the longitudinal vehicle control safer? Insights into speeding and time gaps shorter than one second from a naturalistic driving study with SAE Level 2 automation. Transportation Research Part C 141:103756
claims.quote: When a lead vehicle was detected, drivers were speeding 19.3% of the time (1,085 10-s intervals)

check.note: Section 3.1 is verbatim: 7,175 valid 10-s intervals, a lead vehicle detected throughout in 5,622 of them, speeding in 19.3 % (1,085) of those. 10 drivers; 4 BMW 5 series and 1 Tesla Model S analysed; motorways with limits >= 100 km/h. Speeding was defined as >1 km/h above a 130 limit or >4 km/h above a lower limit, after a 3 % speed correction. The abstract says overall speeding was less likely with ACC+LKS, but more likely when ACC was overridden by the accelerator or long after activation.

claims.quote: The target speed could be regulated manually or directly adjusted to the speed limit detected by the system using the switches (BMW) or the lever (Tesla).

claims.sumo_param: share of vehicles following VSL (e.g. separate compliant vType)
