groups.notes: Derived, not stated in any source (bin midpoints with Sheppard correction; open-ended bins approximated at 47.5 and 92 mph): DfT 2024 motorway cars mean about 68.3 mph (0.976 x the 70 mph limit), sd about 8.5 mph (about 0.12 x limit). Articulated HGVs mean about 54.6 mph (87.8 km/h), sd about 3.4 mph (5.5 km/h), concentrated just under the 56 mph (90 km/h) limiter. Inference for SUMO, unverified: SUMO's default normc(1,0.1) for cars is narrower than GB data and centred higher. GB data come from a 112.7 km/h limit, though. At 100 km/h, NL daytime V85 of minute-averaged lane speeds is 105-108 km/h and DE all-hours mean LVo speed is 99.7 km/h, so the car speedFactor mean at a 100 km/h limit is plausibly at or slightly above 1.0. For trailers, the observed EU pattern (AT semitrailers mean 85.5, V85 88 km/h; GB artic mean 55 mph) fits a narrow desired-speed distribution capped by the 90 km/h limiter. SUMO's default trailer maxSpeed is 130 km/h, so the plant's 90 km/h cap is the binding term. Measurement caveats: RWS V85 is computed from minute-averaged per-lane loop speeds, which understates the individual spread. BASt means are all-hours annual station means, not free-flow filtered. DfT figures are free-flow filtered and exclude smart motorways. The KfV truck table was quoted with whitespace normalised. Several quotes passed through the WebFetch summariser rather than pdftotext: the DfT 2023 page, the LawPlayer ISA text, the Dublin People article, PubMed abstracts and the SUMO docs. Spot-check them against the primary text before citing. The LawPlayer ISA text is a third-party compilation; EUR-Lex was unreachable (empty response). CAV evidence on speed choice conflicts: NL naturalistic L2 driving showed less speeding with ACC+LKS (Varotto 2022), while US L2 driving showed more speeding with ACC (Monfort 2022). ACC set speed is driver-chosen, so CAV-ACC compliance is a behavioural parameter, not a given. For L3 (R157) and ISA speed control, regulations imply speedFactor <= 1 (ISA band: limit - 5 km/h to limit). Field evidence for AV compliance was not found. VSL compliance evidence ranks roughly as follows: enforced UK/DE VSL high (M42 about 85 % at 40 mph at the enforcement threshold); advisory US VAS low (88 % above display, mean +18 km/h); German 1980s static 100 km/h without enforcement 26 %. Downloaded files are in /tmp/claude-1000/-srv-shared-Workspace-phd-phd-speed-harmo-v5b1/31d6d8e5-e88c-4870-9b77-cc7ccfbaac6c/scratchpad/research/speed/ (pdftotext outputs: spe0102.txt, rws_v85_2021.txt, bast_tempolimit.txt, kfv2011_lkw.txt, riggins.txt, aet2009_m42.txt, uba3136.txt, varotto2022.txt, r157am4.txt, dir92_6_consol.txt, i24_marl.txt, tv_vadeby.txt).

groups.title: Perception and information errors at the vehicle level

claims.quantity: Human distance (gap) estimation error, relative (variation coefficient of a log-normal multiplicative error)
claims.value: Vs = 5 % (single value, no distribution; s_est = s·exp(Vs·w_s), w_s a Wiener process of variance 1)
claims.region: n/a (model assumption; authors TU Dresden, Germany)
claims.source: Treiber M., Kesting A., Helbing D., 'Delays, Inaccuracies and Anticipation in Microscopic Traffic Models', arXiv:cond-mat/0404736v3 (3 May 2005), preprint submitted to Physica A (journal pagination not checked in this session)
claims.quote: Relative distance error Vs 5%

check.note: arXiv cond-mat/0404736v3 (3 May 2005), TU Dresden. Sec. 2.2 Eq. (3) reads s_est = s exp(Vs ws) and defines Vs as the variation coefficient. Table 1 lists 'Relative distance error Vs 5%' as a value used in the paper, so it is a model assumption, not a measurement. The paper calls w a 'Wiener process' of variance 1, but its Eq. (5) is an Ornstein-Uhlenbeck-type process.

claims.quantity: Human relative-speed estimation error, modelled as an inverse-TTC error (the error grows in proportion to the gap)
claims.value: rc = 0.01 1/s (single value); (Δv)_est = Δv + s·rc·w_Δv
claims.source: Treiber M., Kesting A., Helbing D., 'Delays, Inaccuracies and Anticipation in Microscopic Traffic Models', arXiv:cond-mat/0404736v3
claims.quote: the uncertainty of the estimation of ∆v is proportional to the distance ... Inverse TTC error rc 0.01/s

check.note: Eq. (4) reads (dv)_est = dv + s rc w_dv. The text says the uncertainty of dv 'is proportional to the distance' (it cites empirical work), and 1/rc is a measure of the TTC estimation error. Table 1 gives 'Inverse TTC error rc 0.01/s' as the value used.

claims.quantity: Correlation time (persistence) of human estimation errors
claims.value: τ = 20 s (single value)
claims.source: Treiber M., Kesting A., Helbing D., 'Delays, Inaccuracies and Anticipation in Microscopic Traffic Models', arXiv:cond-mat/0404736v3
claims.quote: Error correlation time τ 20 s

check.note: Table 1: 'Error correlation time tau 20 s'. Sec. 2.6 says tau is the correlation time of the errors. It is a single assumed value.

claims.quantity: SUMO driver-state device defaults for perception errors (Ornstein-Uhlenbeck error scaled by headway) and change-perception thresholds
claims.sumo_param: device.driverstate.initialAwareness, errorTimeScaleCoefficient, errorNoiseIntensityCoefficient, speedDifferenceErrorCoefficient, headwayErrorCoefficient, speedDifferenceChangePerceptionThreshold, headwayChangePerceptionThreshold, minAwareness, maximalReactionTime
claims.value: initialAwareness 1.0 (no errors at 1); errorTimeScaleCoefficient 100.0; errorNoiseIntensityCoefficient 0.2; speedDifferenceErrorCoefficient 0.15; headwayErrorCoefficient 0.75; freeSpeedErrorCoefficient 0.0; both change-perception thresholds 0.1; minAwareness 0.1. Supported for Krauss, IDM, CACC and ACC; ACC/CACC only with vType applyDriverState=1
claims.source: Eclipse SUMO documentation, 'Driver State' (online version, read 2026-10-28; not version-pinned to 1.27.1)
claims.locator: Parameter table; 'Modeling of Perception Errors'; 'Supported carFollowModels'
claims.quote: speedDifferenceErrorCoefficient | float | 0.15 | Scaling coefficient for the error applied to the speed difference input of the car-following model. | headwayErrorCoefficient | float | 0.75

check.note: Parameter table on the live page matches every value: 1.0, 100.0, 0.2, 0.15, 0.75, freeSpeed 0.0, 0.1, 0.1, minAwareness 0.1, maximalReactionTime = original action step length. The page says perceived gap and speed difference = true + coef*headway*error(t) with an OU process. Supported models for the gap/speed-difference errors: Krauss, IDM, CACC, ACC, with ACC/CACC only when applyDriverState='1'; freeSpeedError works for all models. The page was 'last edited 12 October 2026' and is not pinned to 1.27.1. Its overview still says '(SUMO 1.8.0) only Krauss and IDM' (stale text).

claims.quantity: Literature basis of the SUMO driver-state perception-error model (parameters and validation)
claims.value: c_theta = 100, c_sigma = 0.2, c_x = 0.75, c_v = 0.15, theta_x = theta_v = 0.1 (point values). Checked only visually against one real car-following episode of about 5.5 min from the simTD database, with Krauss accel 1.0, decel 3.0, sigma 0.0, tau 0.72; no fitted distribution
claims.region: EU (Germany; simTD field-test episode used for the visual comparison)
claims.source: Mintsis E. (editor) et al., TransAID D3.1 v2.0 'Modelling, simulation and assessment of vehicle automations and automated vehicles' driver behaviour in mixed traffic', H2020 GA 723390, delivered 19/09/2019
claims.quote: a real car-following episode of an approximate duration of 5.5 min. This episode was extracted from the simTD database ... cθ ≡ 100, and cσ = 0.2 cx = 0.75, and cv = 0.15 θx = θv = 0.1 (math italics normalised)

check.note: TransAID D3.1 v2.0 (delivered 19/09/2019), Sec. 2.3.1.3, pp. 40-42. Eqs. (20)-(25) cover the OU process, eta = c*dx*H, theta = c_theta*A and sigma = c_sigma*(1-A), plus the action-point thresholds. The report quotes c_theta 100, c_sigma 0.2, c_x 0.75, c_v 0.15, theta_x = theta_v = 0.1 and Krauss accel 1.0, decel 3.0, sigma 0.0, tau 0.72, against a simTD episode of about 5.5 min. The comparison is figures only (Figs. 20-22, pp. 43-45); I found no fit statistic. Figs. 21-22 hold awareness constant at A = 0.1, and Fig. 22 uses theta = 0.02.

claims.quantity: Driver awareness just after a transition of control (take-over) and its recovery rate
claims.value: initialAwareness normal(mean 0.7, sd 0.2) truncated to [0.6, 1.0]; recoveryRate normal(0.2, 0.1) truncated to [0.1, 0.5] 1/s (for CV drivers, second iteration)
claims.source: TransAID D3.1 v2.0 (Mintsis E., editor), H2020 GA 723390, 2019
claims.locator: Table 27 'Driver Model parameter values for CVs' (Sec. 3.5)
claims.quote: initialAwareness ... normal(0.7,0.2); [0.6,1.0] ... recoveryRate ... normal(0.2,0.1); [0.1,0.5]

gaps: UK motorway instrumented-vehicle action-point and perception thresholds: Brackstone, Sultan & McDonald 2002 (Transportation Research Part F 5) and Sultan's 2000 Southampton thesis. Full text returned 403/HTML, so no values were read.

Classic relative-speed perception thresholds commonly cited at about 3e-4 to 8e-4 rad/s (Michaels 1963, Todosiev 1963, Evans & Rothery 1977): not read in this session. Only a search summary mentioned the range, so it is not used.

Field-calibrated per-driver or per-vehicle-pair distributions of Wiedemann CC4/CC5/CC6, cars vs trucks (e.g. Durrani, Lee & Maoh 2016, TR-C 67, US NGSIM). The only full text found was an unauthorised copy, so it was not used. A JTE 2019 CC4-CC6 study (ASCE) returned 403.

Numeric headway/distance estimation errors from Taieb-Maimon & Shinar 2001 (Human Factors 43) and Silver & Farber 1968: the abstracts carry no numbers and the SWOV/BGU pages were blocked. Silver & Farber's '7 % at 440 ft' appeared only in a search summary, so it is not used.
The '60 % of actual' TTC underestimation figure often quoted: not verified. The search summary tied it to a separate 1994 Perception paper, not to Hoffmann & Mortimer AAP 1994.
Exact cell means of the perceived/actual TTC ratio in CAMP DOT HS 809 902 sit in figures, not text. Only 'well below 1' and the 0.40-0.70 plot axis were readable.
No field-calibrated distribution of driver awareness for normal (non-take-over) manual driving exists for SUMO's driverstate device. Its defaults rest on one visually compared 5.5-min simTD episode.
No truck-driver-specific perception-error data (distance or relative-speed estimation from a high cab) was found.

No freeway-specific naturalistic distraction prevalence was found as a share of driving time. Dingus 2016 covers all roads; UDRIVE time shares are not split by road type (only the UK share of phone interactions is: 13 % on motorways).

No field measurement of production ACC radar range/range-rate noise against RTK ground truth in car following was found. Only datasheets and a datasheet review (simulation papers assume about 0.25 m / 0.1 m/s).
Bosch LRR4/MRR range and speed accuracy, and current Mobileye EyeQ camera range accuracy: no source found.
The ISO 15622 detection-range requirements (d_max, d_min, d_max_curve) and ISO 22179 (FSRA) lie beyond the free sample. Only tau_min >= 0.8 s was read.
Measured V2V delays in the Ploeg et al. 2011 (ITSC) and Milanés et al. 2014 (IEEE T-ITS) CACC field tests: full text blocked (HAL Anubis, CORE 403, TU/e thesis download blocked).
Field V2X performance under high channel load (dense motorway congestion, many transmitters): not found. All field results above are low-density.
Measured CAM generation-rate distributions at motorway speeds (e.g. Breu et al. 2014, EURASIP JWCN): identified, not read.
GNSS position/speed accuracy carried in CAMs (relevant to CACC gap estimation): not researched.

SUMO 1.27.1-specific check that driverstate errors apply to ACC/CACC with applyDriverState=1: the online doc lists Krauss, IDM, CACC and ACC, but the same page keeps an older line ('Currently (SUMO 1.8.0) it is only implemented for the standard Krauss and IDM'). Verify in the 1.27.1 source.
The Irish RSA mobile-device survey figures are search-snippet only (the RSA pages returned 403).
Production automated-driving lidar (e.g. units fitted to Level 3 cars) and its range/accuracy: not researched.
groups.notes:
Scope and quality. 37 claims: 17 HDV, 20 CAV/V2X. All are FT except the two Hoffmann & Mortimer abstracts (ABS) and the Irish RSA figures (SNIP). Every number was read in this session. Downloads are under /tmp/claude-1000/-srv-shared-Workspace-phd-phd-speed-harmo-v5b1/31d6d8e5-e88c-4870-9b77-cc7ccfbaac6c/scratchpad/research/perception/ (PDFs plus pdftotext .txt). Quotes from layout-extracted PDFs have whitespace collapsed; table quotes join cells with ' | ' or spaces; Unicode math italics in TransAID are normalised.

Key cautions for the plant.
(1) No source gives a field-calibrated distribution for SUMO perception-error parameters. The HDM values (Vs 5 %, rc 0.01/s, 20 s) are author assumptions. The driverstate defaults (0.75/0.15/0.1/100/0.2) were checked only visually against one 5.5-min German simTD episode. The EIDM defaults (sigmagap 0.10, sigmaleader 0.02, tPersEstimate 10 s) are software defaults. Any randomisation of these is an assumption and should be labelled as such, in line with rule E3.
(2) The best experimental anchors for human perception are lab and test-track data: a looming/closing-rate threshold of about 0.003 rad/s and a perceived/actual TTC ratio well below 1 that falls with speed. These support a structural choice (perception thresholds plus a gap-proportional relative-speed error), not specific SUMO coefficients.
(3) Distraction prevalence differs by an order of magnitude across sources and methods: US SHRP2 51.93 % of baselines (any distraction); UDRIVE EU cars 10.2 % of driving time (Germany 1.9 % to Poland 19.4 %), trucks about 20 %; roadside observation of phone use 0.3 % in England (2023) and 6 % in Ireland (2024, SNIP). Definitions are not comparable, and none maps directly to a SUMO parameter. If used, the closest lever is a share of vehicles with driverstate initialAwareness < 1, which would be an assumption.
(4) SUMO mapping. driverstate perception errors are documented for Krauss (the current plant model), IDM, ACC and CACC. ACC/CACC need vType applyDriverState=1, so sensor noise on CAVs could reuse the same device. However, SUMO scales the error linearly with headway, while camera error grows with distance squared (Stein 2003) and radar error is about constant (±0.1-0.4 m). I found no SUMO attribute for V2X latency or packet loss in the CACC model; I believe these would need TraCI/libsumo-side emulation, but this should be verified in the 1.27.1 docs and source.
(5) Sensor magnitudes (manufacturer and review). Radar range accuracy is about 0.1-0.4 m (up to 1.8 m, or 1-5 %), speed accuracy about 0.03-0.28 m/s, cycle 50-80 ms, range 150-250 m. Lidar is 0.02-0.1 m. Monocular camera is about 5 % at 44 m and 10 % at 90 m, with range-rate error about 1 m/s at 30 m. At these levels CAV sensing noise is far smaller than the assumed human errors (HDM's 5 % of gap is 2.5 m at 50 m).
(6) V2X. Field one-way latencies are ITS-G5 about 2-10 ms (median 2.43 ms on the Belgian E313; mode 4 ms in the Dutch CACC tests) and C-V2X PC5 about 20-38 ms. Heavy tails exist: the ITS-G5 99th percentile is 121 ms on E313. PDR is near-certain to about 300 m V2I and to about 480 m V2V; highway NAR stays at or above 90 % to 100-400 m depending on the site. Standards: CAM rate 1-10 Hz (ETSI), V2V latency at most 100 ms (3GPP R14), platooning 10-25 ms at 90-99.99 % (3GPP R15).
My own arithmetic, not a measured value: at 100 km/h (27.8 m/s) the ETSI 4 m position trigger is reached after about 0.14 s. With checks every 100 ms, CAMs would go out about every 0.2 s (about 5 Hz); with faster checks they would approach the 10 Hz cap, subject to DCC.
(7) Not in this group but seen in passing: TransAID D3.1 Tables 26/30 give assumed truncated-normal distributions for Krauss sigma, tau, accel and decel for manual cars and HGVs (simulation assumptions). They are useful to the other groups only as examples of prior practice, not as data.

gaps: Dutch MoniCa/NDW: no verified share of malfunctioning loops or missing-data rate. A search summary attributed '10% of the raw loop data ... unreliable/missing' to a van Lint & Hoogendoorn data-fusion paper, but I did not see the source text. Not used.

Vehicle-length effect on occupancy with European (EU-class) fleets: none found. The only field data are US I-80 (Coifman 2001).

UK/Dutch/German ramp-metering cycle and data-latency specs (e.g. Highways England MCH documents, RWS toeritdosering, German MARZ smoothing): not found before the web-search budget ran out.
End-to-end latency from loop detector to control centre (communication plus processing): no source found. Only aggregation periods (20 s, 30 s, 1 min) are sourced.

Smartphone/consumer GPS positional accuracy (gps.gov page returned 404); commercial probe positional error on motorways: none found. The only positional figure is the Turin urban OBU fleet (mean 6.8 m, sd 13.2 m distance to road).
Kim & Coifman (INRIX vs loop stations), latency 6.8 min: known only through Wang et al.'s citation. Not read directly.
European independent field tests of radar or video counting accuracy on motorways: none found. Only the German TLS acceptance standard and UK radar SVD ground-truth results are available.

CAV-specific sensing for the controller (penetration of CAM-equipped vehicles on EU motorways, CAM positional accuracy, V2X packet loss): not covered. Only the CAM generation rules and OEM traces were sourced.
MIDAS HIOCC/queue-protection algorithm parameters and detector spacing: not searched (search budget exhausted).
groups.notes: The WebSearch budget (shared limit) ran out partway through. The later items came from WebFetch on URLs found earlier, and some gaps above stayed open for that reason. Every claim was read in this session. FT means pdftotext of the downloaded PDF; the PDFs and their text are saved under /tmp/claude-1000/-srv-shared-Workspace-phd-phd-speed-harmo-v5b1/31d6d8e5-e88c-4870-9b77-cc7ccfbaac6c/scratchpad/research/infra/. Caveats: (1) The ALINEA 1991 PDF is an OCR scan, so 'veh/hr' is printed as 'vehlhr' and the Amsterdam distance as '400 min Amsterdam' (read here as 400 m). (2) The NRW missing-data shares are from days already filtered to < 60 % missing, so they understate raw missingness. (3) The PeMS figures (2001-2007) are old and specific to California districts; Rajagopal & Varaiya show large differences between districts (5-40 % failed per day), so a single failure rate would mislead. A two-state per-detector failure process is closer to the data: mostly short outages (about half of failure runs last one day), plus a group of permanently dead detectors (3-24 %). (4) The Knoop 2009 region is inferred from the authors' affiliation; the abstract does not say where. (5) SUMO mapping: E1 induction loops in SUMO 1.27 have no built-in error, failure or latency model, so counts, occupancy and speed should be corrupted in the controller observation layer. Occupancy from E1 depends on vType length, but the loop detection-zone length (the 'effective length') is not added. E1 gives time-mean speed; space-mean speed needs E2/E3 or a harmonic mean. Option names device.fcd.probability / device.fcd.period are my recollection and need checking against the 1.27 docs. (6) Population is 'infrastructure' throughout, as instructed. The CAV angle is covered by probe/FCD penetration, latency and fleet bias (Austrian FCD over-represents trucks: 50 % vs 13 %) and by the ETSI CAM generation rules (100 ms-1 s). (7) Several sources are US-only and 15-20 years old (Middleton/TTI, Coifman); the European sources are TLS 2012 (standard), ORR 2023 (UK availability and radar SVD), the NRW/NDW data papers, and Austria/Italy FCD.

sumo.model_notes:
Basis: docs read from the 1.27.1 Markdown sources (github.com/eclipse-sumo/sumo/tree/v1_27_1/docs/web/docs) and checked against the 1.27.1 C++ source and libsumo 1.27.1 (venv; the system sumo binary is also 1.27.1). The live sumo.dlr.de pages are newer than 1.27.1: they list lcCooperativeHelpThreshold and lcCooperativeMinSpeed, which 1.27.1 does not have. Test files and outputs: /tmp/claude-1000/-srv-shared-Workspace-phd-phd-speed-harmo-v5b1/31d6d8e5-e88c-4870-9b77-cc7ccfbaac6c/scratchpad/research/sumo_map/test/ (probe.py, dyn.py, ds_asl.py, imp.py, out_defaults.json, out_set.json). These were tiny single-vehicle runs at load average below 0.1.

KRAUSS (https://sumo.dlr.de/docs/Definition_of_Vehicles,_Vehicle_Types,_and_Routes.html#default_krauss_model_description)
- Collision-free safe-speed model. Parameters: accel, decel (hard cap), tau, minGap, sigma and sigmaStep. Noise is one-sided dawdling, which lowers mean speed and capacity.
- Supports the driverstate device (tested).
- Robust at 1 s and 0.1 s steps.
- Good HDV baseline for large runs. Weak point: tau is a safety term, not a measured time-gap target, so field time-gap distributions map onto it only loosely.

IDM (same page, parameters table)
- Deterministic in SUMO: sigma is ignored (getImperfection = -1, trajectory identical).
- Parameters a=accel, b=decel, T=tau, s0=minGap, delta, stepping.
- Supports driverstate gap and speed-difference errors (tested).
- Best match to the calibration literature, because published HDV calibrations are mostly IDM-type. I am relying on general knowledge for that statement; verify it per source.
- Docs warn the defaults give very conservative lane-change gap acceptance.
- For heterogeneous HDVs, my reading is IDM + driverstate (noise) + per-vehicle vTypes.

EIDM (https://sumo.dlr.de/docs/Car-Following-Models/EIDM.html; Salles, Kaufmann, Reuss, SUMO Conf. 2020)
- Improved IDM with Human-Driver-Model noise (sigmaerror, sigmagap, sigmaleader, tPersDrive, tPersEstimate), treaction, jerk limits and a drive-off shape.
- Intended for 0.05–0.5 s steps. Incompatible with actionStepLength (it warns).
- Driverstate has NO effect (tested; the calls are commented out in the source).
- May exceed the speed limit temporarily.
- Documentation errors for 1.27.1: sigmaerror defaults to 0.04, not 0.10 (trajectory-verified); the coolness attribute is spelled 'ccoolness', and 'coolness' is silently ignored.
- Results are platform-dependent (randNorm/log).
- Rich HDV realism, but its validation per the reference title is drive-off trajectories against aerial measurements, not freeway car following.

ACC (https://sumo.dlr.de/docs/Car-Following-Models/ACC.html)
- Speed, gap, gap-closing and collision-avoidance modes. tau is the desired time gap; gains are per vType only.
- Hard-coded thresholds, plus a d0 standstill term.
- Docs: collisions at a 1 s step, so use 0.1 s.
- The default gap-closing and collision-avoidance gains were added in TransAID for stable, safe behaviour. The original controller is string-unstable. Gunter et al. 2021 (docs ref 4) report that commercial ACCs are mostly string-unstable. A 'commercial ACC' CAV class should therefore consider the docs' original parametrisation (0.07/0.23, override about 100).
- No sigma. Driverstate only with applyDriverState=1.

CACC (https://sumo.dlr.de/docs/Car-Following-Models/CACC.html)
- Cooperative mode only behind a CACC leader (model-ID check). Otherwise it falls back to an internal ACC with tauCACCToACC (default 1.0, source only).
- Communication is ideal (no delay or loss parameters in 1.27.1).
- The per-vehicle runtime switch is caccCommunicationsOverrideMode.
- vehicle.setTau overwrites both time gaps.
- Use 0.1 s steps.

Calibration of ACC/CACC
- The SUMO docs do not claim that SUMO's ACC/CACC were calibrated to field data by SUMO.
- They state the control laws come from Milanés & Shladover (2014), 'Modeling cooperative and autonomous adaptive cruise control dynamic responses using experimental data', TR-C 48:285–300, doi 10.1016/j.trc.2014.09.001. That title says the models were fitted to experimental data.
- Further sources: Xiao, Wang & van Arem (2017), TRR 2623:1–9, doi 10.3141/2623-01; Xiao, Wang, Schakel & van Arem (2018), TR-C 96:380–397 (CACC only). SUMO integration: Porfyri, Mintsis & Mitsakis (2018), EPiC Series in Engineering 2:82–93, doi 10.29007/r343.
- The only replication the docs claim is qualitative: reproducing the platoon oscillation of Fig. 12 in Milanés & Shladover with the original gains.
- I could not open the 2014 paper (HTTP 403), and the web-search budget for this run was used up. So the test vehicles, test location and whether the default gains equal the published fitted gains are [VERIFY].
- For EU realism the ACC tau and gains would need our own calibration. A JRC open ACC car-following dataset ('OpenACC', Makridis/Mattas/Ciuffo et al.) is a candidate source, from general knowledge only [VERIFY existence, venue and content].

Driverstate support (https://sumo.dlr.de/docs/Driver_State.html)
- Gap and speed-difference perception errors work with Krauss and IDM (tested).
- ACC and CACC only with applyDriverState=1 (tested). EIDM: no effect (tested).
- Default initialAwareness 1.0 gives no errors.
- BUG: maximalReactionTime / actionStepLength scaling under the device is broken in 1.27.1 (remquo rounding plus an inverted mapping; see the row). Keep actionStepLength below 0.8 s at 0.1 s steps, or avoid awareness < 1 with longer ASL, and do not use maximalReactionTime.

Per-vehicle variation, summary
- Only speedFactor takes a distribution inside a vType (norm/normc only).
- Everything else needs a vTypeDistribution of pre-sampled vTypes (createVehTypeDistribution.py), or TraCI setters. The setters create a singular 'type@veh' copy for accel, decel, tau, sigma, minGap, apparentDecel, emergencyDecel, actionStepLength, speedFactor and maxSpeed. LC2013 keys go through vehicle.setParameter('laneChangeModel.*'), except lcSpeedGainUrgency, lcCooperativeHelpTime and lcImpatience.
- Model-specific CF parameters (IDM/EIDM/ACC/CACC) and junction parameters are per vType only, apart from the CACC communication mode.
- Any vType actionStepLength above the step length switches the whole simulation to ballistic update.

Hygiene
- With SUMO_HOME unset, XML schema validation is off, so typos are silently ignored. Run one validation pass with SUMO_HOME pointing at the venv's sumo package and --xml-validation always (tested: it catches 'coolness').
- libsumo prints LC/device parameters with 2 decimals.
- vehicle.setImpatience lasts only until the next step.
